stories.title: 日式老街：鹤见桥商店街
stories.text:
说实话，大阪除了看人流、逛繁华的街区，其余时候有够无聊。反倒是住的地方给了我惊喜。

我们住在西成区的鹤见桥，一条很老、很有生活气息的商店街，跟外面的大阪像是被隔开的两个世界。街上几乎都是老人，每人一辆最普通不过的自行车，不紧不慢地过着自己的日子。邮局、洗衣房、小餐馆、超市应有尽有，过日子根本不用走出这条街。

整条街热闹却宁静，忙碌却透着衰败。在这里能窥见一点日本老人的日常，那是和表面的繁华完全不同的另一面。

小插曲：西成区，中文互联网上疯传的治安混乱之地，没有经验不知道怎么入住民宿，挨个敲邻居的门，把周围房客吓了个半死，最后在某不愿开门只能隔门交流的大姐的帮助下成功入住✌️
stories.textEn:
Honestly, apart from the crowds and the busy shopping districts, Osaka was kind of boring. The real surprise was where we stayed.

Our place was in Tsurumibashi, in Nishinari ward: an old shopping street full of everyday life that feels cut off from the rest of the city, like a different place entirely. Nearly everyone on it is elderly, each riding the plainest bicycle you can imagine, going about their own lives at their own pace. Post office, laundromat, little restaurants, supermarket: you could live your whole life without leaving the street.

It is lively yet quiet, busy yet slowly fading. It gives you a glimpse of how older people in Japan actually live, which is nothing like the glossy surface.

stories.title: 记一家咖啡店的店主奶奶
stories.titleEn: The grandma at the red café
stories.text:
京都，无需多言，完全符合我对这个城市的刻板印象。

从永观堂出来往右走，到一个街角，右手边有一家红色的咖啡店，店主是一位很慈祥的老奶奶。她看我们热得不行又没地方坐，热情地招呼我们进去；语言不通也照样热心招待，看见我们瓶子空了还主动帮我们灌免费的冰水。店里布置得温暖复古，很有格调，门口摆着不少她收藏的老相机。

店里除了奶奶还有一位年轻大婶。我们点了杯饮料，又加了一块蛋糕，看着奶奶从冰箱里小心翼翼地端出手工蛋糕。我们边吃边歇，奶奶在一旁欣慰地看着，用很慈祥的声音念叨着“能好好歇一会儿真是太好了呢，一定热坏了吧”之类的话，时不时还能听到大婶和奶奶之间温馨的家常，背景是和店里氛围刚刚好的音乐。

如果有人告诉我世界上真有这样的场景，要不是亲身经历，我一定会认为那只是动漫里的艺术加工吧。也许等老了，过这样的日子也不错呢。
stories.textEn:
Needs no introduction: exactly as stereotyped.

Turn right out of Eikando and walk to the corner, and on your right is a red café run by a very kind old lady. Seeing us melting in the heat with nowhere to sit, she waved us in. We had no language in common, but she looked after us anyway and kept topping up our free ice water. The place is warm and retro, with a lot of character and a collection of old cameras by the door.

There was also a middle-aged woman helping out. We ordered a drink, then a slice of cake, and watched the grandma carefully lift a homemade cake out of the fridge. While we ate and rested, she watched us contentedly and said in a gentle voice things like "So glad you can have a proper rest, you must be worn out from the heat." Every so often the two of them would chat about everyday things, with music that suited the room perfectly.

If someone had told me scenes like this exist, I would have assumed it was artistic license from an anime. Maybe a life like that, when I'm old, wouldn't be bad at all.

stories.title: 探秘新宿歌舞伎町
stories.text:
歌舞伎町，东京最有名的红灯区，灯红酒绿，亚文化的聚集地。

走进歌舞伎町一番街，满眼都是“无料案内所”，也就是免费介绍各种“服务”的地方。刺眼的霓虹、夸张的招牌、打扮精致的揽客女生，一股脑扑面而来，让人大受震撼。

一番街深处，东宝大楼旁边有一片像广场一样的空地，日本人叫它“トー横”，是亚文化的聚集地。精神小伙、地雷小妹、醉汉、游客、揽客大军、流浪汉，全挤在这一隅：一边是衣衫破旧、无家可归的流浪汉，一边是打扮时髦的人群和繁华的都市夜景，反差之大，冲击力非常强。

穿过一番街继续往北走，就到了大久保公园，传说中的神人公园。不过它早已风光不再，一片广场似的空地被高高的围栏围了起来，旁边紧挨着大久保医院，看上去颇为滑稽。周围站街的也还有，但只剩零星几个。

和大久保公园一样，歌舞伎町的特殊服务也早没了往日的规模。泡泡浴店的营业执照和店面绑定，而且不再新发，楼一旦老化、不再合规，执照也就跟着没了。如今整条街真正“提供服务”的可能只剩一两家，其余大多是素菜荤价，进去只能陪酒聊天。

一路逛下来，离谱的事确实见了不少：聚餐喝多了、在地上撒泼打滚的上班族；独自喝到不省人事、往地上一坐，被陌生路人凑到脸前一顿拍的女生；拐进一条小巷，有人早早打开谷歌翻译专堵中国游客，说能介绍好看的日本女孩陪着喝酒；还有现实里从没见过、在这里随处可见的牛郎店……

这就是繁华背后，东京的另一面。
stories.textEn:
Kabukicho is Tokyo's most famous red-light district: neon, nightlife, and a gathering place for all kinds of subcultures.

Walk into Kabukicho Ichibangai and you are surrounded by "free information centres", shops whose whole job is to point you to whatever service you're after. Blinding neon, outrageous signs, immaculately dressed women touting for customers: it all hits you at once.

Deep inside Ichibangai, beside the Toho building, is an open plaza the Japanese call "Toyoko", a hub for youth subculture. Wannabe tough guys, jirai-kei girls, drunks, tourists, an army of touts and homeless people all crowd into that one corner. On one side, ragged people with nowhere to go; on the other, fashionable crowds and the glittering city. The contrast is staggering.

Keep heading north past Ichibangai and you reach Okubo Park, notorious online for its street scene. Its glory days are long gone: the square-like park is now fenced off with tall barriers, right next to Okubo Hospital, which looks faintly absurd. There are still a few women standing around, but only a handful.

Like the park, Kabukicho's adult industry has shrunk a lot. Soapland licences are tied to the physical premises and no new ones are issued, so as buildings age and fall out of compliance, the licences disappear with them. Today perhaps only one or two places on the whole street still offer the real thing; the rest charge premium prices for drinks and conversation.

I did see plenty of absurd things along the way: office workers so drunk after a work dinner they were rolling around on the ground; a woman alone, passed out sitting on the pavement while strangers shoved phones in her face to take pictures; a tout in a side alley with Google Translate already open, targeting Chinese tourists with offers of pretty Japanese girls to drink with; and host clubs, which I had never seen in real life, on every corner.

This is the other side of Tokyo, behind all the glitter.

stories.title: 睡过去的首都高
stories.titleEn: Night bus, and the Shuto I slept through
stories.text:
为了省路费，顺便再省一晚房费，我们决定坐夜巴，从大阪难波到东京大手町。

车上坐得满满当当，却安静得出奇，每个人都小心翼翼，生怕打扰到别人。邻座是个台湾人，自来熟，却又带着一股日本式的拘谨和礼貌。他在日本读语言学校，暑假出去旅行，学校早就开学了，他今天才往回赶。

夜巴一路走走停停，只在固定的服务区歇脚。哪怕是凌晨，司机也会把所有人叫醒，提醒大家可以下车透透气、上个厕所。天快亮时又停了一站，我困得不省人事，迷迷糊糊下车上了个厕所，一抬头被朝阳美到，随手拍下了这张。

到了终点站，我才后知后觉：刚才那段……是不是首都高 C1？

首都高，东京上空和地下缠成一团的高速路网；C1 都心环状线是其中最短、也最疯的一圈：急弯一个接一个，隧道钻进钻出，路就贴着银座的楼缝穿过去。就这么一圈路，喂饱了《湾岸 Midnight》的漫画、《首都高バトル》的游戏，还有无数个深夜在大黑 PA 集合、掀开引擎盖就能聊到天亮的车友。对一个在赛车游戏里把 C1 跑到闭着眼都知道哪个弯该松油的人来说，这里是圣地，是朝圣的终点站。理论上，此刻耳边应该是直六在隧道里嘶吼、尾灯拉成红线、仪表盘指针一路往右躺。实际上，我坐在一辆规规矩矩守着限速的大巴上，流着口水，睡得正香。
stories.textEn:
To save on the fare, and on a night's accommodation while we were at it, we took a night bus from Namba in Osaka to Otemachi in Tokyo.

The bus was packed but strangely quiet; everyone was careful not to disturb anyone else. The guy next to me was from Taiwan: chatty from the first minute, yet with a very Japanese kind of reserve and politeness. He was at a language school in Japan and had spent the summer travelling; term had already started, and he was only now heading back.

The bus stopped and started all night, pulling in only at fixed service areas. Even in the small hours the driver woke everyone up to say we could get out, stretch, use the toilet. Near dawn we stopped once more. Barely conscious, I stumbled off to the toilet, looked up, was floored by the sunrise, and took this.

Only at the terminal did it hit me: that last stretch... was that the Shuto C1?

The Shuto Expressway is the tangle of highways looping over and under Tokyo, and the C1 inner loop is its shortest and maddest ring: hairpin after hairpin, tunnels in and out, the road threading between the buildings of Ginza. That one loop has fed Wangan Midnight, the Shutokou Battle games, and countless late nights at Daikoku PA where people pop the bonnet and talk until sunrise. For someone who has driven the C1 in racing games until they know every braking point with their eyes shut, this is holy ground, the end of the pilgrimage. In theory, a straight-six should have been screaming through the tunnels, tail lights smeared into red lines, the needle lying flat to the right. In reality, I was on a bus sticking politely to the speed limit, drooling, fast asleep.

Still not over it...

stories.title: 严丝合缝的东京
stories.text:
日本的城市建设，尤其是东京，把建筑工程的美学体现得淋漓尽致：规整，干净，复杂，有序，规模大得离谱，空间利用到了极致。站在高处往下看，整座城就像一盒拼好的乐高，每一块都严丝合缝地卡在该在的位置，多一毫米都塞不进去，少一毫米又显得空。

楼和楼之间架着连廊，高速路从楼缝里钻过去，铁轨底下是商店，商店上面还是铁轨。一块地恨不得用上三遍，看着却一点都不乱，反而有种说不出的舒服。

公共交通也是一绝。线路和车站多到离谱，同一个站能分属好几家公司，换乘一次走出一身汗，看懂线路图之前基本都得迷路几回。但只要摸清楚了，靠电车和地铁真的能解决一切通勤问题。

JY 山手线只能用伟大二字形容，致敬传奇耐拉王🫡一圈 34.5 公里，30 个站，跑完差不多一个小时，东京、上野、池袋、新宿、涩谷、品川，东京最重要的几个地方全被一个圈串起来，高峰期两三分钟就来一趟，客流更是夸张，光新宿站一天进出的人就有三百多万。早高峰的山手线挤爆了，但上下车依然井井有条。尤其留意品川站，那是卫星城社畜们的进城路，小心不要在这一站被挤扁了🤭

最妙的是它的设计，这个圈本身就是骨架：私铁从郊外伸进来，基本都停在圈上，东急在涩谷，小田急和京王在新宿，西武和东武在池袋；圈里面再交给地铁去织网。从郊区来的人在圈上换一次车，就能去城里任何地方。东边那半圈还有京滨东北线贴着并行，很多站同一个站台两边开门，对面就能直接换乘。山手线停运一分钟，东京 GDP 就损失 xx 亿，似乎还真有点可能？另外还有点小浪漫：每个站的发车铃声都不一样，高田马场放的是《铁臂阿童木》，惠比寿放的是惠比寿啤酒的广告曲。坐一圈下来，光听铃声就知道到了哪儿。

所以涩谷站到底什么时候能修好？一个站修十几年也是很有耐心了...

在接下来很长一段时间里，东京依然会是亚洲第一城。
stories.textEn:
Japanese cities, Tokyo above all, show off the beauty of building and engineering like nowhere else: orderly, clean, intricate, precise, absurdly huge, every inch of space put to use. Look down from somewhere high and the whole city is a finished Lego set, every brick clicked into exactly the right spot. Not a millimetre to spare, and not a millimetre missing.

Skybridges link one tower to the next, expressways squeeze through the gaps between buildings, there are shops under the tracks and more tracks above the shops. Each plot of land gets used about three times over, and yet none of it feels messy. If anything it is strangely soothing.

The public transport is something else too. There are absurdly many lines and stations, a single station can belong to several different companies, one transfer is enough to work up a sweat, and you will get lost a few times before the maps make sense. But once you figure it out, trains and the metro really do get you everywhere. And the JY Yamanote Line is nothing short of genius.

It is a closed loop: 34.5 km, 30 stations, about an hour to go all the way round. Tokyo, Ueno, Ikebukuro, Shinjuku, Shibuya, Shinagawa: every place that matters is strung on that one ring. The stations sit incredibly close together, a little over a kilometre apart on average, some just a few hundred metres, so the next one is practically a short walk away. At rush hour a train comes every two or three minutes, so nobody looks at a timetable; miss one and you just take the next. Go the wrong way and who cares: clockwise is sotomawari, anticlockwise is uchimawari, it is a circle either way, you just ride half a loop more 😂

The crowds are unreal. Shinjuku alone sees more than three million people pass through every day, making it the busiest station in the world. The morning rush packs the Yamanote like a tin of sardines, and yet getting on and off stays perfectly orderly: no pushing, no shouting, the doors open and close and a whole carriage of people is swapped in a few seconds.

The cleverest part is the design. The loop is the skeleton: private railways run in from the suburbs and mostly stop right on the ring, Tokyu at Shibuya, Odakyu and Keio at Shinjuku, Seibu and Tobu at Ikebukuro, while the metro weaves the network inside it. Come in from the suburbs, change once on the ring, and you can reach anywhere in the city. On the eastern half the Keihin-Tohoku Line runs right alongside, and at many stations the two share a platform, so you just walk across to change.

And a little romance: every station has its own departure jingle. Takadanobaba plays the Astro Boy theme, Ebisu plays the old Yebisu beer advert tune. Ride a full loop and you can tell where you are from the music alone.

So when is Shibuya Station ever going to be finished? Hoardings and temporary passages everywhere, and the exits seem to move every time you come back.

For a long time to come, Tokyo will still be the greatest city in Asia.

stories.title: 俄罗斯与东正教
stories.titleEn: Russian Orthodoxy: the people who stand
stories.text:
在俄罗斯待久了，教堂是绕不开的。城里走不了几条街就能看见一个金顶，过节的时候门口总有人排队。一开始只是进去拍照，后来跟着去了几次礼拜，复活节熬了一个通宵，慢慢也对这套东西起了兴趣。

先说来历。988 年，基辅罗斯的弗拉基米尔大公受洗，信仰从拜占庭传过来，圣像、礼仪、教堂的样子也一并搬了过来。1453 年君士坦丁堡陷落，莫斯科开始把自己当成正教的继承人，有了“第三罗马”的说法，1589 年设了自己的牧首。后来彼得大帝嫌教会碍事，干脆把牧首废了，改由政府控制的主教公会来管，一直到 1917 年才恢复。

真正的劫难在苏联时期。新政权要的是无神论：教堂被拆、被封，或者改成仓库、工厂、俱乐部，神父被枪毙、被流放的数以万计。到 1939 年，全国还开着门的教堂只剩几百座。莫斯科的救世主大教堂 1931 年被直接炸掉，原地本来要盖苏维埃宫，没盖成，最后挖成了一个露天游泳池，一游就是三十多年。圣彼得堡那边，喀山大教堂变成了宗教与无神论历史博物馆，圣以撒大教堂里挂起傅科摆，用来演示地球自己在转，滴血大教堂当过存菜的仓库。二战时斯大林为了凝聚人心松过一次口，1943 年允许重新选牧首；到了赫鲁晓夫手里又收紧，再关掉一大批。

转机在八十年代末。1988 年罗斯受洗一千年，教会第一次被允许公开纪念；苏联解体以后，教堂一座座被还回来、修起来。救世主大教堂按原样重建，2000 年祝圣；滴血大教堂的马赛克前前后后修了二十多年。现在看到的那些金碧辉煌，不少其实是最近三十年的事。

东正教堂和天主教堂长得很不一样。外面最显眼的是洋葱顶，个数有讲究：一个是基督，三个是三位一体，五个是基督加四位福音书作者。进到里面，没有长椅，所有人从头站到尾；也没有管风琴，只有人声。正前方是一整面挂满圣像的墙，叫圣障，把祭坛和信众隔开，正中那扇门只有神职人员能走。墙上、穹顶上画满了画，中央穹顶上通常是全能者基督往下看着。东正教不立雕像，只敬圣像。莫斯科也有天主教堂，红砖哥特式，里面一排排长椅，从东正教堂出来再进去，反差特别大。

最让我感兴趣的是那一大堆规矩。女人进门要包头巾、穿裙子，男人要摘帽子。画十字要三根手指并拢，从额头到胸口，再从右肩点到左肩，跟天主教正好反过来。进门先买蜡烛，插到想求的那位圣人像前，再弯腰亲吻圣像。一场礼拜动辄两三个小时，中途有人来有人走，有人一直站着，有人跪下去磕头。

东正教还用旧历，所以圣诞节在 1 月 7 日。那天在圣彼得堡的喀山大教堂，里面挤得转不开身，空气里全是蜡烛和香的味道。复活节则是一年里最大的节，前面有七个星期的大斋，不吃肉蛋奶。节前一天，大家提着篮子来教堂，里面装着复活节面包、奶渣甜点和染好的彩蛋，排队等神父洒圣水。重头戏在半夜：教堂里站满了人，挤不进去的就在外面等，快到零点时，神父举着十字架和圣像带头，所有人捧着蜡烛绕教堂走一圈，这叫十字游行。回到门口，神父喊“基督复活了！”，所有人齐声回“真的复活了！”，一晚上要来回喊好多遍。礼拜一直持续到凌晨，散场时大家互相亲脸、交换彩蛋。第二天街上熟人见面，打招呼也换成了这两句。

一月底又去了一次礼拜，赶上的是三圣师节，纪念大巴西勒、神学家格里高利和金口约翰三位圣师。那天印象最深的是唱诗。东正教不用乐器，全靠唱诗班：男低音沉得像从地底下冒出来，女声在上面一层层铺开，再和穹顶的回声叠在一起，站在底下会起鸡皮疙瘩。拉赫玛尼诺夫那部《彻夜晚祷》就是从这种唱法里来的。教会斯拉夫语一句也听不懂，但一点不影响被它震住。

再说说看到的现状。教堂是修好了，信的人却在变少。调查里自认东正教徒的人有七成上下，可真正每个月都去教堂的只是很小一部分。礼拜上大多是中老年人，尤其是老太太；年轻人里，除非家里本来就信、从小被带着去，信的人不多。更常见的是另一种人：脖子上挂着十字架，手腕上戴着圣像手链，复活节也会去点根蜡烛、分块面包，可斋戒、告解、每周礼拜这些基本做不到。问起来，他们会说自己是信的，只是信在心里。信仰还在，那套繁复的教规已经不怎么管得住人了。

另一边，新教堂还在盖。莫斯科郊外库宾卡的武装力量主教堂 2020 年才建成，去的那天里面正好有人在办婚礼，新娘的头纱拖在地上好几米。在教堂办婚礼的年轻人不少，对他们中的很多人来说，这大概更像一场隆重的仪式。

我不信教，很多规矩到现在也没完全弄懂。不过每次站在人群后面听唱诗，还是会想多待一会儿。作为个人符号偶尔拿出来彰显个性，也是个不错的选择。
stories.textEn:
Spend long enough in Russia and you cannot avoid the churches. Every few streets there is another golden dome, and on holidays there is always a line at the door. At first I only went in to take pictures. Then I tagged along to a few services, stayed up all night for Easter, and slowly got hooked.

Some background first. In 988 Grand Prince Vladimir of Kievan Rus was baptized, and the faith arrived from Byzantium along with its icons, its liturgy and the shape of its churches. After Constantinople fell in 1453, Moscow began to see itself as the heir of Orthodoxy, the "Third Rome", and in 1589 it got its own patriarch. Peter the Great later found the church inconvenient, abolished the patriarchate and put a state-run Holy Synod in charge. The patriarchate only came back in 1917.

The real catastrophe came under the Soviets. The new state wanted atheism: churches were torn down, shut, or turned into warehouses, factories and clubs, and tens of thousands of priests were shot or exiled. By 1939 only a few hundred churches were still open in the whole country. In Moscow, the Cathedral of Christ the Saviour was blown up in 1931 to make way for a Palace of Soviets that was never built; the site ended up as an open-air swimming pool for more than thirty years. In Saint Petersburg, Kazan Cathedral became a Museum of the History of Religion and Atheism, St Isaac's hung a Foucault pendulum to show the earth turning on its own, and the Church of the Savior on Spilled Blood was used to store vegetables. Stalin eased off during the war to rally the country and allowed a new patriarch in 1943; Khrushchev tightened the screws again and closed another wave of churches.

The turn came in the late 1980s. In 1988 the church was allowed to celebrate the millennium of the baptism of Rus in public, and after the Soviet Union fell the churches were handed back and restored one by one. Christ the Saviour was rebuilt to the old design and consecrated in 2000; the mosaics of Spilled Blood took more than twenty years to restore. A lot of the gold you see today is only about thirty years old.

Orthodox churches look nothing like Catholic ones. From outside, it is the onion domes, and their number means something: one for Christ, three for the Trinity, five for Christ and the four Evangelists. Inside there are no pews, so everyone stands from start to finish, and there is no organ, only voices. Across the front stands a wall covered in icons, the iconostasis, which separates the altar from the congregation; only clergy may pass through its central doors. Walls and domes are painted all over, and from the central dome Christ Pantocrator usually looks down. There are no statues, only icons. Moscow does have a Catholic cathedral, red-brick Gothic with rows of benches, and walking into it straight from an Orthodox church is quite a contrast.

What fascinated me most were the rules. Women cover their heads and wear skirts, men take off their hats. You cross yourself with three fingers together, forehead to chest, then right shoulder to left, the opposite of Catholics. You buy a candle at the door, place it before the icon of the saint you are praying to, and bend to kiss the icon. Services easily run two or three hours; people drift in and out, some stand the whole time, some kneel and touch their foreheads to the floor. The first time I went I spent ages just watching when everyone else crossed themselves and bowed, afraid of getting it wrong.

The Orthodox church still follows the old calendar, so Christmas falls on January 7. I spent it in Kazan Cathedral in Saint Petersburg, packed so tight you could barely turn around, the air thick with candle smoke and incense. Easter is the biggest feast of the year, preceded by seven weeks of Lent without meat, eggs or dairy. The day before, people bring baskets of Easter bread, sweet curd paskha and dyed eggs and queue for the priest to sprinkle them with holy water. The main event is at midnight: the church is full, those who cannot get in wait outside, and just before twelve the priests lead everyone, candles in hand, around the church behind the cross and icons. Back at the doors the priest calls out "Christ is risen!" and the crowd answers "Truly He is risen!", again and again through the night. The service runs until the early hours, and afterwards people kiss each other's cheeks and swap eggs. The next day, those same two lines replace "hello" on the street.

At the end of January I went to another service, for the feast of the Three Holy Hierarchs: Basil the Great, Gregory the Theologian and John Chrysostom. What stayed with me was the singing. The Orthodox church uses no instruments, only the choir: basses so low they seem to rise out of the floor, women's voices layered on top, all of it folding into the echo of the dome. Standing underneath it gave me goosebumps. Rachmaninoff's All-Night Vigil grew out of exactly this kind of singing. I did not understand a word of Church Slavonic, and it did not matter at all.

Now, what I saw of the present. The churches have been restored, but the believers are thinning out. In surveys around seventy percent call themselves Orthodox, yet only a small fraction go to church even once a month. Services are mostly middle-aged and older people, especially grandmothers. Among the young, unless the family is religious and brought them along as children, few really believe. More common is another kind: a cross around the neck, an icon bracelet on the wrist, a candle and a slice of Easter bread at Easter, but fasting, confession and weekly services are mostly out of reach. Ask them and they will say they do believe, just in their own way. The faith is still there; the elaborate rules no longer hold people the way they did.

Meanwhile, new churches keep going up. The Main Cathedral of the Russian Armed Forces in Kubinka, outside Moscow, was only finished in 2020. The day I went there was a wedding inside, the bride's veil trailing metres across the floor. Plenty of young couples marry in church, and for many of them it is probably more of a grand ceremony than anything else.

I am not religious, and I still have not figured out half the rules. But every time I stand at the back of the crowd and listen to the choir, I want to stay a little longer.

stories.title: 俄罗斯美学：一层压着一层
stories.text:
这一年多在俄罗斯拍的建筑放在一起，很难说哪一种才算“俄罗斯风格”。木头尖顶、洋葱顶、意大利人修的城墙、彼得堡的巴洛克、斯大林的尖塔、赫鲁晓夫的板楼、玻璃幕墙的摩天楼，全都挤在同一个国家，甚至同一条街上。俄罗斯的审美不是顺着一条线慢慢长出来的，更像是一层一层盖上去的：每隔一两百年，国家就猛地换一次方向，新的一层压上来，旧的一层却很少被彻底拆掉。

最底下一层是木头。俄罗斯中部森林多、石头少，几百年里教堂、宫殿、农舍几乎都是木造的，很多后来被当成“俄罗斯特色”的形状，最早都是木匠的办法：陡峭的帐篷顶好搭，又不积雪；屋檐和窗框上满是雕花，一家比一家讲究。莫斯科南边的科洛缅斯科耶有一座阿列克谢沙皇的木宫，原物 1768 年就因为朽坏被拆了，2010 年才照着留下来的测绘图重新盖起来。里面的墙从上到下画满花草，窗户不是玻璃，是一小片一小片云母拼的。同一个园子里还有一座 1532 年的耶稣升天教堂，用砖把木结构的帐篷顶原样搬了上去，是最早的石造帐篷顶教堂之一。

再一样是颜色。一年里有小半年是白雪、灰天和下午四点就黑透的夜，在这样的底色上，天蓝的墙、绿色的屋顶、金色的十字架格外显眼。苏兹达尔的木屋刷成蓝的、黄的，教堂的洋葱顶有金的、绿的，还有蓝底撒金星的。洋葱顶为什么长成这样，说法很多：防积雪、像烛火、从拜占庭的穹顶慢慢演变过来，至今没有定论，但它在雪地里确实远远就能认出来。

第二层来自拜占庭。988 年罗斯受洗，一起接过来的还有一整套对待光的方式：教堂里的金色不是装饰，是神的光，所以圣像的背景、穹顶的马赛克都铺满了金。外面越冷越暗，里面越要金碧辉煌。这一点一千年来几乎没变过，从新耶路撒冷修道院圆形大殿里斜照下来的光，到滴血大教堂满墙的马赛克，再到 2020 年才建成的武装力量主教堂，进门的感受都差不多：先是一片暗，然后被金色和烛光包住。

有意思的是，最“俄罗斯”的东西常常出自外国人之手。十五世纪末，伊凡三世请来一批意大利建筑师重修克里姆林宫，红砖城墙上那一排燕尾形的城垛，其实是米兰的样式。到了彼得大帝，干脆在涅瓦河口的沼泽上新造了一座欧洲城市。圣彼得堡从一开始就是做给欧洲看的：先是拉斯特雷利的巴洛克，黄墙、白柱、金顶，彼得霍夫大宫的教堂就是这一路；接着是越来越严整的古典主义，海军部的金色尖顶，花了四十年才盖完的圣以撒大教堂。很长时间里城里的楼都不许高过冬宫，所以彼得堡的天际线平得出奇，只有几根金色尖顶戳出来。宫殿里的大厅和长廊也是同一个思路：照着欧洲最好的做，再做得更大、更满。

十九世纪，风向又转了回来。打败拿破仑以后，俄罗斯开始认真找“自己的样子”，尼古拉一世时期的官方口号是“东正教、专制、民族性”。建筑师托恩把拜占庭和古罗斯的元素拼成一种新风格，盖了大克里姆林宫和第一座救世主大教堂。到了 1870 到 1890 年代，红场边上一座接一座冒出红砖、尖顶、雕花窗框的大楼：国家历史博物馆、上商场（也就是现在的古姆）、市杜马大楼。它们看着古老，其实和埃菲尔铁塔差不多是同一时期的，古姆那个铁和玻璃的拱顶出自工程师舒霍夫，用的是当时最新的技术。伊古姆诺夫宅邸那种像从童话书里走出来的房子，也是这时候盖的；滴血大教堂则是同一个思路在彼得堡的版本，有意和周围的欧式街道格格不入。

1917 年以后的头十几年，苏联建筑其实走在世界的最前面，构成主义的工人俱乐部、公社住宅、舒霍夫的镂空钢塔，都是那时候的东西，可惜这次没拍到几张。转折发生在 1930 年代初。1931 年救世主大教堂被炸掉，原地要盖一座四百多米高、顶上站着列宁像的苏维埃宫；1932 年各种艺术团体被统一解散，之后只剩“社会主义现实主义”一条路。建筑要“民族的形式，社会主义的内容”，说白了就是要宏伟、要好懂，要让每个人一看就知道国家有多强大。苏维埃宫最后没盖成，但它的气质被分给了后来的一大批建筑。

第一批成果在地下。1935 年莫斯科地铁通车，定位是“人民的地下宫殿”：大理石、马赛克、水晶吊灯、青铜雕像，统统搬到地下几十米。环线的基辅站 1954 年开通，拱顶上一幅幅镶着石膏花边的壁画，讲的是俄罗斯和乌克兰的“友谊”；很多站里都有工人、农民、士兵的群像，有的还镀了金。对刚从农村涌进城里的人来说，每天上下班都从这样的大厅里穿过，这本身就是宣传。

战后是“七姐妹”。1947 年莫斯科建城 800 周年那天，八座高楼同时奠基，最后盖成了七座：莫斯科大学主楼、外交部、乌克兰酒店、科捷利尼切斯卡亚滨河公寓、库德林广场大楼、列宁格勒酒店和红门大楼。它们的路数几乎一样：底下是厚重的古典柱式，中段层层收进，顶上一根尖塔加一颗红星，墙面上是麦穗、国徽和花环。说它学的是纽约的摩天楼也好，学的是克里姆林宫的塔楼也好，都对，这正是斯大林式样的特点：什么都拿来，再全部放大到纪念碑的尺度。外交部大楼的尖顶，据说是斯大林看了图纸以后让加上去的。第八座本来要盖在红场旁边的扎里亚季耶，地基都打好了，后来改盖了俄罗斯酒店，酒店拆掉以后，那里成了一座公园，秋天有人坐在那里写生。

同样的逻辑放大到一整片园区，就是全俄展览中心。它 1939 年开放，1954 年整体重建成现在的样子：凯旋门式的正门上，拖拉机手和集体农庄女庄员高举麦捆；每个加盟共和国一座展馆，用各自的民族纹样装饰，有的贴花砖，有的贴彩陶，合起来就是“各民族大家庭”的样板间。人民友谊喷泉的十六个金色姑娘，代表当时的十六个加盟共和国。园区边上立着穆希娜 1937 年为巴黎世博会做的《工人与集体农庄女庄员》，再往外是 1964 年的太空征服者纪念碑，一道一百多米高的钛合金尾焰直冲上天。苏联的纪念碑偏爱这种动势，人物永远在迈步、举臂、往前冲，摩尔曼斯克港口上的“阿廖沙”也是这样，三十多米高，面朝大海站着。

这一切在 1955 年被叫停。斯大林死后两年，赫鲁晓夫的政府发布了《关于消除设计和建筑中的浪费现象》的决议，批评的正是这些尖塔和柱廊。接下来的几十年，苏联用预制板盖起了海量的住宅，先是五层的“赫鲁晓夫楼”，再是九层、十六层的板楼，从莫斯科一路盖到北极圈里的摩尔曼斯克。今天走在俄罗斯任何一座城市的外围，看到的大多还是这一层：一模一样的楼，靠刷成不同的颜色来区分。审美在这里让位给了数量，可也正是这一层，让几千万人第一次住进了自己的公寓。

苏联解体以后，前面几层同时回来了。教堂一座座重建，莫斯科从 2010 年起还在推一个在新住宅区补建两百座教堂的计划；全俄展览中心修旧如旧，重新刷金；莫斯科城的玻璃塔楼一座比一座高，彼得堡郊外的拉赫塔中心 2019 年建成，成了欧洲最高的楼；新修的大环线地铁，把扶梯井做成了喷气发动机的样子。看起来像是在告别苏联，可很多习惯其实没变：国家依然是最大的甲方，建筑依然要讲一个宏大的故事。武装力量主教堂最能说明这一点。它是东正教堂，却刷成军装的绿色，主穹顶直径 19.45 米，钟楼高 75 米，小穹顶直径 14.18 米，分别对应 1945 年、胜利 75 周年和卫国战争的 1418 天。这种用数字说话的办法，和胜利公园里那座 141.8 米高的方尖碑如出一辙。

人的穿着打扮也是这个脾气。冬天街上是毛皮帽和长大衣，颜色大多很暗，可一到剧院、节日，大家就格外隆重，好像要把平日的灰都补回来。民族服饰这几年又流行起来：帕夫洛沃波萨德的印花羊毛头巾，十九世纪就是这个样子，现在年轻姑娘也拿来配大衣；夏天林子里的民俗节上，有人穿着红色的斜领衬衫弹琴，女孩穿着萨拉凡长裙跳舞。红色、金色、大朵的花，和建筑上用的是同一套颜色。人和衣服以后再单独写。

要说这些层之间有什么共同点，大概是它们都更在乎被很多人看见，而不是让一个人住得舒服。木教堂要在平原上老远就能望见，金顶要在雪地里发亮，七姐妹要从城里任何一个角落都看得到，就连板楼也是按“全体人民”的尺度来算的。俄罗斯的美很少是精巧的、私密的，它是公共的，往大里做的，有时候让人觉得压迫，有时候又确实动人。
stories.textEn:
Put together all the buildings I photographed in Russia over the past year or so, and it is hard to say which of them counts as the “Russian style.” Wooden spires, onion domes, city walls built by Italians, Petersburg baroque, Stalin’s spires, Khrushchev’s panel blocks and glass skyscrapers all crowd into the same country, sometimes the same street. Russian taste did not grow slowly along a single line. It was built up in layers: every century or two the state abruptly changed course, a new layer was laid on top, and the old one was rarely torn down completely.

The bottom layer is wood. Central Russia has plenty of forest and little stone, so for centuries churches, palaces and farmhouses were almost all built of timber, and many shapes later seen as typically Russian began as carpenters’ solutions. A steep tent roof is easy to raise and sheds snow; eaves and window frames were covered in carving, each house trying to outdo the next. At Kolomenskoye, south of Moscow, stands the wooden palace of Tsar Alexei. The original was so rotten that it was pulled down in 1768, and it was only rebuilt in 2010 from the surviving survey drawings. Inside, the walls are painted with flowers from floor to ceiling, and the windows are not glass but small pieces of mica fitted together. In the same park is the Church of the Ascension of 1532, which carried the wooden tent roof over into brick and is one of the earliest tent-roofed churches in stone.

Then there is colour. For almost half the year the background is white snow, grey sky and nights that are fully dark by four in the afternoon, and against it sky-blue walls, green roofs and gold crosses stand out sharply. In Suzdal the wooden houses are painted blue and yellow, and church domes come in gold, in green, or in blue scattered with gold stars. There are many theories about why the domes are onion-shaped: to keep snow off, to look like a candle flame, or as a slow evolution of the Byzantine dome. None is settled, but in the snow you can certainly spot one from far away.

The second layer came from Byzantium. When Rus was baptised in 988, it took over a whole way of treating light along with the faith. Gold in a church is not decoration but divine light, which is why icon backgrounds and dome mosaics are covered in it. The colder and darker it is outside, the more radiant the inside has to be. That has hardly changed in a thousand years. From the light slanting into the rotunda of the New Jerusalem Monastery to the mosaic-covered walls of the Church on Spilled Blood and the Main Cathedral of the Armed Forces, finished only in 2020, the feeling on entering is much the same: darkness first, then you are wrapped in gold and candlelight.

The odd thing is how often the most “Russian” things were made by foreigners. In the late fifteenth century Ivan III brought in a group of Italian architects to rebuild the Kremlin, and the swallowtail battlements along its red brick walls are in fact a Milanese design. Peter the Great went further and built a brand-new European city on the marshes of the Neva delta. Saint Petersburg was made from the start to be seen by Europe: first Rastrelli’s baroque of yellow walls, white columns and gilded domes, as in the church of the Grand Palace at Peterhof, then an ever stricter classicism, with the Admiralty’s golden spire and Saint Isaac’s Cathedral, which took forty years to build. For a long time nothing in the city was allowed to rise above the Winter Palace, so the Petersburg skyline is strikingly flat, broken only by a few gold spires. The palace halls and galleries follow the same idea: copy the best of Europe, then make it bigger and fuller.

In the nineteenth century the wind turned again. After defeating Napoleon, Russia began to look seriously for a face of its own, and the official slogan under Nicholas I was “Orthodoxy, Autocracy, Nationality.” The architect Konstantin Thon combined Byzantine and Old Russian elements into a new style and built the Grand Kremlin Palace and the first Cathedral of Christ the Saviour. In the 1870s to 1890s, red brick buildings with spires and carved window frames rose one after another around Red Square: the State Historical Museum, the Upper Trading Rows (today’s GUM), the City Duma. They look ancient but are roughly contemporary with the Eiffel Tower, and GUM’s iron-and-glass roof was designed by the engineer Vladimir Shukhov using the newest technology of the day. Fairy-tale houses like the Igumnov House date from the same period, and the Church on Spilled Blood is the Petersburg version of the same idea, deliberately out of step with the European streets around it.

For the first ten-odd years after 1917, Soviet architecture was in fact at the front of the world, with constructivist workers’ clubs, communal housing and Shukhov’s lattice steel tower; sadly I took few pictures of that period. The turning point came in the early 1930s. In 1931 the Cathedral of Christ the Saviour was blown up to make way for a Palace of Soviets more than four hundred metres tall, topped by a statue of Lenin. In 1932 all the independent art groups were dissolved, leaving only the path of socialist realism. Architecture had to be “national in form, socialist in content,” which in plain terms meant grand, easy to read, and able to show anyone at a glance how powerful the state was. The Palace of Soviets was never built, but its spirit was handed down to a whole generation of buildings.

The first results were underground. The Moscow Metro opened in 1935 and was pitched as “underground palaces for the people”: marble, mosaics, crystal chandeliers and bronze statues were all carried dozens of metres below ground. Kievskaya on the Circle Line opened in 1954, and the murals in their plaster frames along its vault tell the story of Russian–Ukrainian “friendship.” Many stations have groups of workers, peasants and soldiers, some of them gilded. For people who had just poured into the city from the countryside, passing through halls like these on the way to and from work every day was propaganda in itself.

After the war came the “Seven Sisters.” On Moscow’s 800th anniversary in 1947, foundation stones were laid for eight tall buildings, and seven were finished: the main building of Moscow State University, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Hotel Ukraina, the Kotelnicheskaya Embankment apartments, the Kudrinskaya Square building, the Leningradskaya Hotel and the Red Gates building. They share almost the same recipe: heavy classical orders at the bottom, setbacks in the middle, a spire with a red star on top, and wheat ears, coats of arms and wreaths on the walls. You could say they borrowed from New York skyscrapers or from the towers of the Kremlin, and both would be right. That is the mark of the Stalinist style: take everything, then blow it all up to the scale of a monument. The spire on the Foreign Ministry was reportedly added after Stalin saw the drawings. The eighth tower was meant for Zaryadye, next to Red Square. Its foundations were already laid when the site was given to the Hotel Rossiya instead; after the hotel was demolished it became a park, where people sit and sketch in autumn.

Apply the same logic to an entire park and you get VDNKh, the Exhibition of Achievements of the National Economy. It opened in 1939 and was rebuilt into its present form in 1954. On top of the triumphal-arch gate, a tractor driver and a collective-farm woman hold up a sheaf of wheat. Each Soviet republic had its own pavilion decorated with its own national patterns, some in tile, some in majolica, together forming a showroom of the “family of peoples.” The sixteen golden maidens of the Friendship of Peoples Fountain stand for the sixteen republics of the time. Next to the grounds is Vera Mukhina’s Worker and Kolkhoz Woman, made for the 1937 Paris Exposition, and further on the 1964 Monument to the Conquerors of Space, a titanium rocket trail more than a hundred metres high. Soviet monuments love this kind of motion: the figures are always striding, raising an arm, surging forward. “Alyosha” above the port of Murmansk is the same, more than thirty metres tall and facing the sea.

All of this was stopped in 1955. Two years after Stalin’s death, Khrushchev’s government issued its decree “On the Elimination of Excesses in Design and Construction,” aimed squarely at those spires and colonnades. Over the following decades the Soviet Union built an enormous amount of housing from prefabricated panels, first the five-storey “khrushchyovkas,” then nine- and sixteen-storey blocks, from Moscow all the way to Murmansk inside the Arctic Circle. Walk around the edge of any Russian city today and this is the layer you mostly see: identical blocks told apart only by the colours they are painted. Here aesthetics gave way to numbers, yet it was this layer that gave tens of millions of people a flat of their own for the first time.

After the Soviet collapse, all the earlier layers came back at once. Churches were rebuilt one after another, and since 2010 Moscow has been running a programme to add two hundred churches to new residential districts. VDNKh was restored to look as it once did, gold and all. The glass towers of Moscow City keep getting taller, the Lakhta Center outside Petersburg became the tallest building in Europe in 2019, and the new Big Circle Line of the metro has an escalator shaft shaped like a jet engine. It looks like a farewell to the Soviet era, but many habits have not changed: the state is still the biggest client, and buildings still have to tell a grand story. The Main Cathedral of the Armed Forces shows this best. It is an Orthodox church painted in uniform green; its main dome is 19.45 metres across, its bell tower 75 metres high and its small dome 14.18 metres across, standing for 1945, the 75th anniversary of victory and the 1,418 days of the war. Speaking through numbers like this is exactly what the 141.8-metre obelisk in Victory Park does.

Dress follows the same temperament. In winter the streets are full of fur hats and long coats, mostly in dark colours, but for the theatre or a holiday people dress up remarkably, as if making up for all the grey of ordinary days. Folk dress has come back into fashion in recent years. The printed wool shawls of Pavlovsky Posad look as they did in the nineteenth century, and young women now wear them over their coats. At a summer folk festival in the woods, a man in a red side-buttoned shirt played music and a girl danced in a sarafan. Red, gold and big flowers: the same palette as the buildings. People and clothing will get a story of their own later.

If these layers have anything in common, it is probably that they care more about being seen by many people than about being comfortable for one. A wooden church had to be visible from far across the plain, gold domes had to shine in the snow, the Seven Sisters had to be visible from every corner of the city, and even the panel blocks were measured on the scale of “the whole people.” Russian beauty is rarely delicate or private. It is public and built big, at times oppressive, and at times genuinely moving.

stories.title: 俄罗斯 mentality
stories.titleEn: The Russian mentality: put your hat on first
stories.text:
“mentality”这个词不好翻译成中文。说“心态”太轻，说“国民性”又太重，大概就是一群人共同的脾气。在俄罗斯待了一年多，交了不少朋友，也被不少陌生人帮过、夸过、教育过。下面所记的都是我自己碰到的真人真事，不算结论，只是一个来自外国人视角的观察。

先从穿衣服说起。俄罗斯人出门很在意自己的样子，哪怕只是去趟超市，很多人也要收拾一番。冬天尤其讲究，讲究的重点是分层：贴身一层保暖内衣，中间毛衣或抓绒，外面一件长羽绒服或大衣，再加上帽子、围巾、手套，室外是一台精致，室内又是另一套精致。外面零下十几二十度，室内因为集中供暖，二十多度是常事，穿着大衣坐在屋里根本待不住，所以进门第一件事就是脱大衣。剧院、博物馆、餐厅、学校，门口都有衣帽间，有专人收大衣、发号码牌，穿着大衣往里走，多半会被叫回来。去朋友家也一样，主人总是一进门就催你把外套脱了。

他们对“穿对”的执着，有时真是让人哭笑不得。有一次没戴帽子出门，走在街上，一个素不相识的路人拦住我，一脸认真地问我怎么不戴帽子🤣在很多俄罗斯人看来，冬天不戴帽子就是在拿脑袋开玩笑，迟早要生病。我只好说忘了，对方摇摇头走了，那表情像是在看一个不懂事的孩子。

讲究的另一面是精致。冬天街上能看到不少女生，裹着厚厚的羽绒服，帽子和围巾配好颜色，妆容一丝不苟，从上到下白得发光，精致得像瓷娃娃。

还有一点很重要：这里的女孩子大多喜欢把自己打扮得成熟一些，女孩子两三岁话都说不明白妈妈就开始给她们化妆，夸人年轻要小心。一个不太严谨的规律：在街上看到一个女生，如果你觉得她 25 岁，那她大概 18 岁；如果你觉得她 18 岁，那她大概只有 14 岁⚡️得益于斯拉夫人强大的基因，俄罗斯娃娃基本就没有不好看的。花期短也可能是事实，不过我认为主要还是取决于个人的生活习惯。

第一次去莫斯科大剧院，看的是《天鹅湖》。进门存大衣的时候才发现不对劲：周围几乎每个人都盛装打扮，男士西装革履，女士长裙高跟，一个个看起来就像贵族老爷和夫人。我们几个穿得随随便便，夹在中间格格不入，确实尴尬。好在灯一暗，就没人在意我们了。我们坐在很高的楼座，几乎是俯视舞台，看不清演员的脸，却能把整个队形看得清清楚楚：湖边的天鹅在蓝光里排开，几十个人像一个人一样起落，乐池就在脚下。演出真的非常精彩。后来我才明白，对俄罗斯人来说，去剧院本身就是一件值得打扮的事。

反过来也成立：好好打扮之后出门，真的会收到意想不到的关注和善意。男生会直接走过来搭讪，女生会投来目光，老爷爷老奶奶会冲你微笑致意。说实话，还挺受用😋这种街头小插曲很有欧美的味道：夸你就是为了夸你，搭讪就是为了搭讪，说两句就走，不留联系方式，也不等你多回应。目的性可能很强，又装作一点也不强，我到现在也没找到一个合适的词来形容它。

在亲密关系这件事上，俄罗斯人也很开放。情侣随处拥抱接吻，旁若无人，让我一度以为这不是什么大不了的事。直到有一次，我把镜头对准了一对已经抱着亲了十几分钟的情侣，结果被他们追上来，要求检查我有没有拍到过于亲密的画面...看来旁若无人，也只是在没人拍的时候。

俄罗斯人在街上很少笑，地铁里一整节车厢的人都板着脸，刚来的人很容易觉得他们冷漠。笑在这里是留给熟人的，对陌生人无缘无故地笑，反而会显得奇怪。可一旦成了朋友，就完全是另一副样子：热情，讲义气，你的事就是他们的事。对陌生人其实也一样，只是方式很别扭。我受过许多陌生人的帮助，几乎都是同一个套路：一句话不多说，默默停下来帮忙，帮完就自顾自走开，连句谢谢都来不及听。这种傲娇属性（？）属实有点可爱。

几个朋友还带我去过不少酒吧、清吧、舞池和文化俱乐部，这种夜里的文化在年轻人里非常流行。有的地方很文艺，墙上画满涂鸦，大家围着桌子聊天、念诗、弹吉他，谁想唱就唱一首；有的地方就疯得不行，通宵喝酒、蹦迪、社交，手腕上盖个章进去，出来的时候天已经亮了。夏天莫斯科的夜很短，九点多天黑，凌晨三四点天就开始发白，街上还有人三三两两地往下一家走。疯完那几回，我终于知道了什么叫 Moscow never sleeps。

城市之外又是另一番样子。今年夏天，朋友邀请我去他在莫斯科郊外的一处小宅子，正好赶上村里的一个节日庆典。村民们穿着民族服饰，女人包着大花头巾、穿着长裙，男人穿着绣花衬衫；大家一起编花环、骑马、射箭、围成圈跳舞，孩子们上台唱歌，队伍敲着鼓穿过田野，到了晚上再点起篝火。这里的村民多才多艺，热情好客，对我这个端着相机到处跑的外国人也毫不见外。那两天体验到了很多在城里见不到的东西，也拍出了不少我很喜欢的人文照片。第二天早上，朋友家的桌上摆着一盆樱桃、一盆草莓，院子里的樱桃树上还挂着果子。

我交友算是很广，上至家境富裕的社会精英，下至街头的精神小伙，都有接触。每个阶层过着怎样的生活，大概也了解了不少：住在哪里，周末去哪，钱花在什么上，对未来怎么打算，差别大得像是在不同的国家。但有一件事几乎所有人都一样：炫耀性消费非常流行。买大牌，很重要的目的就是让人看见，豪车停在路边，就是要让整条街都看到。而且没有人对此感到羞耻，也没有人觉得这样很装：有钱，为什么不让人知道？

另一件让很多人自豪的事，是盗版。电影、游戏、软件，能不花钱就不花钱，大家聊起来一点也不心虚，反而有点得意，好像这就是俄罗斯人聪明能干的证明。制裁以后很多西方公司撤出，想买正版也买不到，这份自豪就更理直气壮了。

网上一直流传一种说法：东欧女生里精神状态不太健康的比例偏高，很多和原生家庭有关，比如父亲过于强势。我一直将信将疑，觉得这种标签太粗暴。直到后来，一个女性朋友向我吐露了她长期以来的烦恼，还有她糟糕的精神和身体状况，极度的社交焦虑，需要看心理医生和吃药来维持正常。在此之前她给人的感觉一直是自信大方。她说的很多东西，也引起了我自己的一些共鸣，而多多少少有着类似经历的人，我还认识好几个。我依然不觉得能从一个个体推出一个民族的全貌，但从那以后，再看到街上那些打扮得一丝不苟的人，我会想，他们背后是不是也有些不愿提及的经历。

东正教的影响则更像一层底色。真正常去教堂的人不多，可很多人脖子上挂着十字架，家里摆着圣像，复活节会分彩蛋，进教堂时女生会自觉包上头巾。问起来，他们大多会说自己是东正教徒，信不信是另一回事，这更像是身份的一部分。

同一个国家里，圣彼得堡人的精神状态尤其与众不同。他们更偏欧洲人气质，更多元，更热情开放，也更自由主义。有一次我在一个圣彼得堡人面前介绍自己来自莫斯科，他马上说他早就看出来了，每个从莫斯科来的人都像我这样，而我到现在也不知道“像我这样”是什么样。

这份优越感背后，其实是整个国家的心结。俄罗斯人自古以来就渴求西方世界的认可，从彼得大帝在沼泽上造出一座欧洲城市开始，“我们算不算欧洲”就是一个反复出现的问题，圣彼得堡人独特的身份认同，有一部分就来自这里。这几年的制裁，让俄罗斯基本放弃了融入西方的幻想，开始倒向中国。政府的宣传也确实让中国人在这里非常受待见：莫斯科过春节，红场挂满红灯笼办起庙会，红旗取代迈巴赫成为豪华轿车优选。

可年轻人未必跟着宣传走。我接触到的 Z 世代，对政治越来越不满，很多人在认真考虑离开这个国家。社会也在一点点变化，只是很少有人会在公开场合说出来。

东亚文化在年轻人里很流行，但不太能上桌吃饭：喜欢的人很多，却很少被当成严肃的东西。流行的主要是这几样：中国的佛教、二游和其他一些文化符号，韩国的 K-pop，日本的二次元。商场里有整面墙的漫画和手办，扭蛋机前围着小孩，街上偶尔还能看到贴满动漫美少女的痛车。

写到这里，愈发认识到一个人可以多复杂，不同的文化间可以有多么不同。也许 mentality 本来就是这样一团说不清的东西。在这里待得越久，我越不敢下结论，只能先把平时看到的记录下来。
stories.textEn:
“Mentality” doesn't translate neatly into Chinese. “Attitude” is too light, “national character” too heavy; it's roughly the temper a group of people share. In over a year in Russia I made plenty of friends and was helped, complimented and lectured by plenty of strangers. What follows is only what I ran into myself: not conclusions, just one foreigner's observations.

Start with clothes. Russians care a lot about how they look when they go out; even for a trip to the supermarket, many people make an effort. Winter is where it gets serious, and the point is layers: thermal underwear, then a sweater or fleece, then a long down coat or overcoat, plus hat, scarf and gloves. It comes down to climate and heating. Outside it's ten or twenty below; inside, thanks to central heating, it's often over twenty degrees, and you can't sit there in a coat. So the first thing you do indoors is take it off. Theatres, museums, restaurants and schools all have a cloakroom by the door, with someone taking coats and handing out numbered tags; walk in wearing yours and you'll probably be called back. Visiting friends is the same: the host will urge you out of your coat the moment you step in.

Their devotion to dressing right sometimes left me baffled and amused at once. Once I went out without a hat, and a complete stranger stopped me in the street and asked, quite seriously, why I wasn't wearing one. To many Russians, going hatless in winter is gambling with your head, and you'll get sick sooner or later. I said I'd forgotten; they shook their head and walked off, looking at me like a child who didn't know better.

The other side of all that care is polish. In winter you see plenty of young women wrapped in thick down coats, hat and scarf colour-matched, make-up flawless, cheeks red from the cold, as delicate as porcelain dolls. Kids come in bright one-piece snowsuits and roll around in the snow without a care.

Something else took me a long time to get used to: most girls here like to dress older than they are. So be careful about calling someone young; what sounds like flattery to us may not land as a compliment at all. My not-very-scientific rule of thumb: if a girl on the street looks 25 to you, she is probably 18; if she looks 18, she is probably only 14.

My first time at the Bolshoi Theatre was for Swan Lake. Only when we checked our coats did I realise something was off: almost everyone was dressed to the nines, men in suits, women in long gowns and heels, every one of them looking like a lord or lady. The few of us in our everyday clothes stuck out badly, and it really was awkward. Luckily, once the lights went down nobody cared. We sat high up in the upper tiers, looking almost straight down on the stage: you couldn't see the dancers' faces, but you could see the whole formation, the swans spread out across the blue-lit lake, dozens of dancers rising and falling as one, the orchestra pit right below us. The performance was truly wonderful. I later understood that for Russians, going to the theatre is itself an occasion worth dressing up for.

The reverse holds too: dress up properly and go out, and you get unexpected attention and kindness. Guys walk straight up to start a conversation, girls glance your way, old men and women smile and nod. Honestly, I rather enjoyed it. These little street episodes feel very Western: a compliment is just a compliment, a chat-up is just a chat-up, and then they're gone, no number, no waiting for much of a reply. Maybe there's a clear purpose behind it, while pretending there isn't; I still haven't found the right word for it.

Russians are also very open about affection. Couples hug and kiss anywhere, as if no one else were around, and after seeing it so often I came to think it was no big deal. Until one time I pointed my camera at a couple who had been locked in a kiss for a good ten minutes, and they came after me and asked to check that I hadn't captured anything too intimate. As if no one else were around, apparently, only applies when no one is taking pictures.

Russians rarely smile in the street, and a whole metro carriage of straight faces can make newcomers think they're cold. Smiles here are kept for people you know; smiling at strangers for no reason just seems odd. But once you're friends, they're completely different: warm, loyal, treating your problems as their own. Even with strangers it's the same, only expressed awkwardly. I've been helped by many strangers, and it almost always goes the same way: no words, they just stop and help, then walk off on their own before you can even say thanks. That tsundere streak is honestly a bit adorable.

Friends also took me to plenty of bars, quiet lounges, dance floors and cultural clubs; this night culture is hugely popular with young people. Some places are artsy, walls covered in graffiti, people around a table talking, reading poetry, playing guitar, anyone singing if they feel like it. Others are completely wild: drinking, dancing and socialising all night, a stamp on your wrist going in, and daylight when you come out. Summer nights in Moscow are short; by three or four the sky is already paling, and people are still drifting in twos and threes to the next place. Those nights, I finally understood what “Moscow never sleeps” means.

Outside the city is another world. This summer a friend invited me to his small house outside Moscow, just in time for a village festival. The villagers wore traditional dress, women in big floral headscarves and long skirts, men in embroidered shirts; everyone wove flower wreaths, tried archery and danced in circles, children sang on stage, a procession beat drums across the fields, and at night they lit a bonfire. The villagers were talented and hospitable, and didn't treat me, a foreigner running around with a camera, as an outsider at all. Those two days showed me a lot you never see in the city, and I came away with many people photos I love. The next morning, my friend's table had a bowl of cherries and a bowl of strawberries, with more cherries still hanging on the tree in the yard.

My circle of friends is wide, from the children of wealthy elites to the tracksuited street lads, and I got a decent sense of how each layer of society lives: where they live, where they go at weekends, what they spend on, how they plan for the future. The differences are so big it's like different countries. But one thing is almost universal: conspicuous consumption is everywhere. A big part of buying luxury brands is being seen; a supercar parked on the street is meant to be noticed by the whole block. And nobody feels ashamed of it or thinks it's pretentious: if you have money, why not let people know?

Another thing many people are proud of is piracy. Films, games, software: if you don't have to pay, you don't, and people talk about it with no guilt at all, almost smugly, as if it proved how clever and resourceful Russians are. Since the sanctions many Western companies have left, so you couldn't buy the legal version even if you wanted to, which makes the pride all the more righteous.

There's an idea that keeps circulating online: that an unusually high share of Eastern European women struggle with their mental health, often because of their families, an overbearing father, for instance. I was always half sceptical; the label felt too crude. Then a female friend opened up to me about the troubles she'd carried for years, and about her poor mental and physical health. A lot of what she said struck a chord with me too. I still don't think you can generalise from one person to a nation, but since then, when I see people in the street dressed immaculately, I sometimes wonder what they might be carrying.

Orthodoxy is more like a base coat. Not many people go to church regularly, but many wear a cross around their neck, keep icons at home, share eggs at Easter, and women cover their heads without being told when they enter a church. Ask them and most will say they're Orthodox; whether they believe is another matter. It's more a part of identity. I wrote about this in “The people who stand”, so I won't go into it again here.

Within the same country, people from St Petersburg have a distinctly different vibe: more European, more diverse, warmer and more open, more liberal. Once I introduced myself to someone from Petersburg as coming from Moscow, and he said straight away that he'd already guessed; everyone from Moscow is like me. I still don't know what “like me” means, but judging by his face, it probably wasn't a compliment.

Behind that sense of superiority is a knot in the whole country. Russians crave recognition from the West. Ever since Peter the Great built a European city on a swamp, “are we Europe or not?” has been a recurring question, and part of Petersburg's distinctive identity comes from it. The sanctions of recent years have more or less ended the dream of joining the West, and the country has turned toward China. Government messaging really has made Chinese people very welcome here: at Chinese New Year the centre of Moscow is hung with red lanterns for a temple fair, and Chinese cars sit on display in shopping-mall atriums.

Young people don't necessarily follow the messaging, though. The Gen Z Russians I know are increasingly unhappy with politics, and many are seriously thinking about leaving the country. Society is slowly changing too, though few people will say so in public.

East Asian culture is popular among young people but doesn't quite get a seat at the table: lots of fans, but rarely taken seriously. What's popular is mainly Chinese Buddhism, anime-style mobile games and other Chinese cultural symbols, Korean K-pop, and Japanese anime and manga. Malls have whole walls of manga and figures, kids crowd around the gacha machines, and now and then you see a car wrapped in anime girls.

Writing all this down, I notice how much of it contradicts itself: cold to strangers, warm to friends; immaculately dressed by day, wild by night; longing for the West's approval while turning to embrace the East; showing off unapologetically, yet not necessarily at ease inside. Maybe a mentality is just that, a tangle you can't quite put into words. The longer I stay, the less I dare draw conclusions; all I can do is write down what I've seen.

stories.title: 金子做的城，和撑起它的人
stories.titleEn: Dubai: the city of gold, and the people holding it up
stories.text:
落地迪拜的第一天早上，我站在谢赫扎耶德路边上。十几条车道从楼群中间穿过去，两边的高楼一栋比一栋高、一栋比一栋怪，薄雾把它们泡得像海市蜃楼。很难相信，五十多年前这里还只是波斯湾边上一个靠采珍珠、跑货船过日子的小渔港。

阿联酋 1971 年才建国，由七个酋长国组成，迪拜和阿布扎比是其中最大的两个。很多人以为迪拜的钱都是从地底下抽出来的，其实全国绝大部分石油都在阿布扎比；迪拜自己的石油早就不多了，如今石油在迪拜经济里的占比还不到百分之一。迪拜的钱来自贸易、航空、旅游、房地产和金融：这里不收个人所得税，开着全球最繁忙的国际机场之一，还有中东最大的港口。它用了几十年，把自己从一个"没什么油的酋长国"做成了全世界有钱人和打工人都想来的地方。

繁华在这里是看得见、摸得着的。828 米的哈利法塔，世界最高楼，站在城里任何地方抬头都能看到它；朱美拉棕榈岛是硬生生从海里填出来的，从高处往下看，一片棕榈叶的形状铺在海面上，叶子上挤满了别墅；未来博物馆像一只刻满阿拉伯书法的银色眼睛；迪拜商场里有一整面墙的瀑布，还有一个巨大的水族箱，鲨鱼和鳐鱼就在逛街的人头顶上游。

去了一家叫 First Motors 的超跑车行，布加迪、劳斯莱斯、阿斯顿马丁女武神……这些平时只在海报上见到的车，在这里像超市货架上的商品一样一排排摆着，门口路边停着的也大多不是凡品。

阿布扎比是另一种气质：更安静，也更"官方"。阿布扎比卢浮宫的穹顶把阳光筛成一场光雨落在水面上；总统府金碧辉煌，吊灯大得像一座倒挂的宫殿；谢赫扎耶德大清真寺入夜后打上蓝光，倒映在水里，白得不像人间的建筑。

可是这些楼是谁盖的？这座城每天是谁在运转？

阿联酋大约一千万人口，真正持有阿联酋国籍的本地人只占一成左右，剩下近九成都是外国人。其中最多的是印度人，第二多的就是巴基斯坦人，接着是孟加拉、菲律宾、埃及……在迪拜街头，你很难碰到一个本地人，倒是满街的南亚面孔：工地上、出租车里、送外卖的摩托上、超市收银台后面。

两种人过着两种生活。本地公民从出生起就有免费的医疗和教育，结婚有补贴，成家有政府分的地或住房贷款，很多人在政府部门或国企拿着体面的薪水。而外来务工人员的签证绑定在雇主身上（"卡法拉"担保制度），一个普通建筑工人一个月挣一两千迪拉姆，折合人民币三四千块，住在城郊的劳工营里，几个人甚至十几个人一间屋；夏天气温四五十度，法律规定中午那几个小时不许在户外干活——需要专门立法来规定这件事，本身就说明了一些问题。他们挣的钱大多汇回老家：巴基斯坦每年从海湾国家收到大量侨汇，阿联酋是最主要的来源之一。有人付出几百倍的汗水，换来勉强生存的条件，而本地人不费吹灰之力就过上了安逸幸福的一生。

有一晚十二点，我在迪拜城边一条很偏的路上，看到一群人在路边的台阶上随地一坐，就这么聊着天。起初我以为就是一群在外打工的"精神小伙"，下班了没地方去，在路边吹吹风，让我给他们拍了张合照。

拍完细看才发现：手表、金链子、手链、戒指……一群看起来很有钱的人，半夜十二点在荒郊僻壤一条昏暗的路边席地而坐聊天。过于魔幻了。

迪拜就是这样：贫穷和富有在这里不总是一眼就分得清，它们有时候就坐在同一条台阶上。

在迪拜，巴基斯坦人真的很多。就连去了沙漠，遇到并拍下的也是巴基斯坦人。而且巴基斯坦人是真的很喜欢中国人，一听说你是中国人，热情就上来了。

让我印象最深的，是在朱美拉海滩遇到的一家人。

一个小女孩和她的爸爸妈妈，他们是巴基斯坦人。爸爸在迪拜工作，妈妈和孩子平时都在巴基斯坦，这次是一家人难得的团聚；再过几个月家人就要回去，到时候爸爸又会是一个人。那天上午阳光很好，小女孩穿着救生衣在浅水里扑腾，爸爸跟在她旁边游，笑得合不拢嘴。我给他们家拍了一些照片。

后来的事情就没那么美好了。爸爸似乎着了魔一样，对我表现出疯狂的热情，聊天的内容也越来越过线。他三番五次希望我再去迪拜，一直想和我视频。我们没有共用的能视频通话的社交软件，我说可以用 Instagram，他却一直不愿意。我说不清这是文化差异，是巴基斯坦人太喜欢中国人，还是他个人的问题。但站在一个中国人的角度，我认为这已经可以定性为骚扰了。
后来实在没招了，他才说可以用 IG。加上关注后一看，果然和我猜想的一样：他的 IG 发布的内容、关注的人，都是一副想要寻找另一段亲密关系的样子，那正是他不想让我看到的东西。

可我又会想起那个上午：一家人在海滩上其乐融融，他说起家人快要走了时脸上的失落，还有他对女儿近乎疯狂的爱——他的动态里几乎全是女儿。这些都太真实了。这些复杂的、互相矛盾的真实拼在一起，才是他：一个在迪拜工作的巴基斯坦人。

我不知道家人不在的时候，他究竟过着怎样的生活。也许就像网上说的那样，在一座金子做的城里，日复一日地出卖力气，换一个勉强体面的生存；把最好的那一面留给每年见一次的女儿，把剩下的孤独、欲望和不堪，留在没人看见的地方。

迪拜的繁华是真的，哈利法塔、棕榈岛、满街的超跑都是真的。撑起这一切的人，也是真的。
stories.textEn:
On my first morning in Dubai I stood beside Sheikh Zayed Road. More than a dozen lanes cut through a canyon of towers, each taller and stranger than the last, and the haze made them look like a mirage. It is hard to believe that fifty-odd years ago this was a small fishing port on the Persian Gulf, living off pearl diving and trading boats.

The UAE only became a country in 1971, a federation of seven emirates, of which Dubai and Abu Dhabi are the largest. Many people assume Dubai's money comes out of the ground, but most of the country's oil is in Abu Dhabi; Dubai's own oil ran low long ago, and today it makes up less than one percent of Dubai's economy. Dubai's money comes from trade, aviation, tourism, real estate and finance: there is no personal income tax, it runs one of the world's busiest international airports and the largest port in the Middle East. In a few decades it turned itself from "the emirate without much oil" into a place where the world's rich and the world's workers all want to be.

Here, wealth is something you can see and touch. The 828-metre Burj Khalifa, the tallest building in the world, is visible from almost anywhere in the city. Palm Jumeirah was dredged up out of the sea; from above, a palm frond lies on the water, every leaf crowded with villas. The Museum of the Future looks like a silver eye carved with Arabic calligraphy. Dubai Mall has a waterfall the height of a wall and an aquarium so large that sharks and rays swim above the shoppers.

I visited a supercar dealer called First Motors: Bugatti, Rolls-Royce, an Aston Martin Valkyrie… cars I had only ever seen on posters, lined up like goods on supermarket shelves. Even the cars parked on the street outside were nothing ordinary.

Abu Dhabi has a different temperament: quieter, more official. The dome of the Louvre Abu Dhabi sifts the sunlight into a rain of light on the water; the Presidential Palace glitters with gold, its chandeliers like upside-down palaces; and at night the Sheikh Zayed Grand Mosque is lit blue and reflected in the pools, too white to look like something built by people.

But who built these towers? And who keeps this city running every day?

The UAE has about ten million people, and only around one in ten actually holds Emirati citizenship. Nearly nine in ten are foreigners. Indians are the largest group, Pakistanis the second, followed by Bangladeshis, Filipinos, Egyptians… On the streets of Dubai you rarely meet a local, but South Asian faces are everywhere: on building sites, behind the wheel of taxis, on delivery motorbikes, behind supermarket tills.

Two kinds of people live two kinds of lives. Emirati citizens get free healthcare and education from birth, grants when they marry, land or housing loans from the state when they start a family, and many hold comfortable jobs in government or state companies. Migrant workers' visas, meanwhile, are tied to their employers (a system called kafala, loosened somewhat in recent years). An ordinary construction worker earns one or two thousand dirhams a month, about three or four thousand yuan, and lives in a labour camp on the edge of the city, several or even a dozen to a room. Summer temperatures reach the mid-forties and above, and the law forbids outdoor work during the hottest hours of midday; the fact that a law is needed for that says something on its own. Most of what they earn is sent home: Pakistan receives huge remittances from the Gulf every year, and the UAE is one of the biggest sources.

There is a harsh line online: some people pour in hundreds of times the sweat just to scrape by, while the locals glide into a comfortable, happy life without lifting a finger. Before I came I thought that was an exaggeration. After coming, I couldn't argue with it.

One night at midnight, on a remote road at the edge of Dubai, I came across a group of men sitting right on the kerb, just chatting. At first I took them for young migrant workers with nowhere to go after their shift, catching some air by the road, and I took a group photo of them.

Only when I looked closely afterwards did I notice: the watch, the gold chain, the bracelet, the rings… a group of men who looked rather well off, sitting on the ground on a dim, out-of-the-way roadside at midnight, chatting. Surreal.

That is Dubai: poverty and wealth are not always easy to tell apart here; sometimes they sit on the same step.

There really are a lot of Pakistanis in Dubai. Even out in the desert, the people I met and photographed were Pakistanis. And Pakistanis really do love Chinese people; the moment they hear you're Chinese, the warmth switches on. "Iron brothers," as the Chinese internet calls Pakistan, is more than a meme here.

What I can't put down is the family I met on Jumeirah Beach.

A little girl and her father, from Pakistan. The father works in Dubai; the mother and daughter usually live in Pakistan, and this was a rare family reunion. In a few months they would go home, and the father would be alone again. The sun was lovely that morning; the girl splashed in the shallows in her life jacket while her father swam beside her, grinning from ear to ear. I took some photos of the family for free.

What came after was less lovely. The father seemed almost possessed, showering me with frantic enthusiasm, and our chats crossed more and more lines. Again and again he wanted me to come back to Dubai, and kept asking to video call. We had no app in common for video calls; I suggested Instagram, and he kept refusing. When he ran out of options, he finally agreed to IG. One look confirmed what I'd guessed: the posts on his account and the people he followed all said he was looking for another intimate relationship. That was exactly what he hadn't wanted me to see.

I can't tell whether this was a cultural difference, Pakistanis liking Chinese people too much, or just him. But from where I stand, as someone from China, I would call it harassment.

And yet I keep thinking of that morning: the family happy together on the beach, the disappointment on his face when he mentioned his family leaving soon, and his almost obsessive love for his daughter; nearly everything he posts is about her. All of it is too real. These complicated, contradictory truths, put together, are him: a Pakistani man working in Dubai.

I don't know what his life is like when his family isn't there. Maybe it is just what people say online: in a city made of gold, selling his labour day after day for a barely decent living; saving his best self for the daughter he sees once a year, and leaving the loneliness, the desire and the ugliness somewhere nobody can see.

At night the Burj Khalifa is lit up, and the whole city is still glowing.

Dubai's wealth is real. The Burj Khalifa, the Palm, the supercars on every street are all real. And so are the people holding it all up.

stories.title: 迪拜的车
stories.titleEn: Dubai showrooms: two dealers, a lifetime of dream cars
stories.text:
迪拜这次最疯狂的一天，是在车行里度过的。先后逛了两家，First Motors，和它隔壁的 Pupil of Fate Motors。一进门就发现，平时在游戏里开了无数圈的熟悉面孔，全在这里，一切是那么不真实。

先说我最喜欢的两辆。

第一辆是 Aston Martin Valkyrie。Adrian Newey 把 F1 的空气动力学思路直接搬进了公路车，6.5 升自然吸气 V12，转速能拉到 1 万 1 以上，公路版全球只有 150 台。亲眼看到才明白，照片里的样子是真的：车身几乎全是曲面和气道，每一寸都在做事，轮毂上那圈荧光黄，在哑光黑的衬托下像一条刀口。

[图]

第二辆是 Porsche 911 GT3 RS，我心目中最顶的车，没有之一。三四台不同配色，车身侧面贴着大大的 GT3 RS 字样。我喜欢它，是因为它很纯粹，凝聚着保时捷品牌一直以来的独特气质：4.0 升自然吸气水平对置六缸，9000 转，再加上夸张的主动尾翼，一台还能每天开出门的赛道车。在一屋子几百万、上千万的超跑中间，这几台 911 一点也不输气势，反而是我拍得最久的。

[图]

First Motors 里，McLaren P1 一黑一红就放在不远的地方，红黑那台是 P1 GTR，原本只能在赛道上跑，全球只有 58 台，尾翼高高翘起的样子实在太帅了。另一台是普通的 P1，375 台。

[图]

[图]

Porsche 918 Spyder，全球 918 台，荧光黄的卡钳至今我还觉得是最好看的一种配色。

[图]

红色的 Ford GT，福特当年想买还要先过审核，一共约 1350 台。尾部那两个大排气管，像要把站在后面的人吸进去。

[图]

旁边是 KTM X-Bow GT-XR，没车顶没车门，限量 100 台，简直是把赛车直接牵上了路。

[图]

用红色围栏圈起来的那一片是法拉利。Enzo，400 台，是法拉利纪念创始人的作品，旁边是黄色的 812 Competizione，V12 转速直奔 9500，限量 999 台。

[图]

LaFerrari，499 台。旁边还有它的敞篷版 Aperta，全球只有 209 台，居然还是黄色的。

[图]

Bugatti 也在这里：蓝色的 Divo，全球只有 40 台，据说发布前就被抢购一空；旁边是白色的 Chiron，W16 引擎 1500 马力。

[图]

灰色的 Mercedes-AMG ONE，直接把 F1 引擎装进街车，限量 275 台，纽北最速量产车。

[图]

灰色的 Aventador SVJ 63，为纪念兰博基尼成立 63 周年只做了 63 台，车头还有一个专属的小标志。

[图]

薄荷绿的 Rolls-Royce Cullinan 夹在中间，在满屋子的超跑里反而最有个性。

[图]

黑色的 Lamborghini Sián Roadster，兰博基尼第一台混动，敞篷版只有 19 台，金色轮毂配黑色车身，太帅了。

[图]

最后是 McLaren Speedtail，三座布局、驾驶位在正中间，一共 106 台，那个长长的泪滴形车身很有未来感。

[图]

隔壁的 Pupil of Fate 灯更亮，落地玻璃，车摆得也松，像一个展厅。一进门就看到一台绿色的 Speedtail，这个颜色我从来没见过。

[图]

然后是三台 McLaren Senna，浅蓝的、黑白的，还有一张近拍尾部。500 台，名字来自传奇车手塞纳，每个细节都是为赛道准备的。

[图]

[图]

黑色的 Lamborghini Centenario，为创始人 100 岁诞辰而造，硬顶版只有 40 台。

[图]

这里还有两台 Valkyrie，灰色配黄色线条，和 First Motors 那台黑色的各有各的好看，我又愣了一会。

[图]

AMG ONE 在这里又见到两台，蓝色蜂窝涂装那台尤其特别。

[图]

深蓝色的 Bugatti Chiron 配橙色轮毂，大胆，但真的好看。

[图]

玻璃门后面安静地停着一台红色的 Ferrari 550 Maranello，前置 V12 加手动挡，现在已经买不到这种老派 GT 了。

[图]

最后是 Ferrari Monza SP，没有挡风玻璃，复古造型，SP1 和 SP2 加起来一共 499 台。

[图]

接下来是幻想时间🥹
stories.textEn:
The craziest day of this Dubai trip was spent inside car showrooms. I visited two, First Motors and Pupil of Fate Motors right next door. I thought I'd seen some good cars, but the moment I walked in, everything I'd only seen in pictures and videos was right there, a metre away.

Let me start with my two favourites.

First, the Aston Martin Valkyrie. Adrian Newey took F1 aerodynamic thinking and put it on the road, with a 6.5-litre naturally aspirated V12 that revs past 11,000 rpm. Only 150 road cars exist. Seeing it in person, I understood that the look in the photos is real: the body is almost all curves and air channels, every inch doing a job, and the fluorescent yellow ring on the wheel looks like a knife edge against the matte black.

[图]

Second, the Porsche 911 GT3 RS, my dream car, no contest. Three or four of them in different colours, with big GT3 RS lettering down the side. I love it because it's so pure, and it carries everything Porsche has always stood for: a 4.0-litre naturally aspirated flat-six that goes to 9,000 rpm, a huge active wing, a track car you can still drive out the door every day. Among millions of dollars of supercars, these 911s held their own, and they're the ones I photographed the longest.

[图]

At First Motors, a black and a red McLaren P1 stand not far apart. The red-and-black one is the P1 GTR, track-only originally, just 58 built, and the way its wing sticks up is so cool. The other is a regular P1, 375 built.

[图]

[图]

The Porsche 918 Spyder, 918 built, and the acid-yellow brake calipers are still one of my favourite colour choices ever.

[图]

The red Ford GT. Ford made buyers go through an approval process, and about 1,350 were built. The two big exhausts at the back look like they could suck in whoever stands behind.

[图]

Next to it, the KTM X-Bow GT-XR, no roof and no doors, limited to 100, basically a race car led onto the road.

[图]

The area ringed with red ropes is Ferrari. The Enzo, 400 built, made in honour of Ferrari's founder, and beside it the yellow 812 Competizione, with a V12 heading for 9,500 rpm, limited to 999.

[图]

The LaFerrari, 499 built. Beside it is its open-top Aperta sibling, only 209 in the world, and in yellow no less.

[图]

Bugatti is here too: the blue Divo, only 40 built and reportedly sold out before it was even announced, and next to it a white Chiron with a W16 and 1,500 horsepower.

[图]

The grey Mercedes-AMG ONE puts an F1 engine in a road car, limited to 275, and the fastest production car around the Nürburgring.

[图]

The grey Aventador SVJ 63, built for Lamborghini's 63rd anniversary, only 63 made, with a little special badge on the nose.

[图]

A mint-green Rolls-Royce Cullinan sits among them and, in a room full of supercars, has the most personality.

[图]

The black Lamborghini Sián Roadster, Lamborghini's first hybrid, only 19 roadsters, gold wheels on a black body, so cool.

[图]

Last is the McLaren Speedtail, three seats with the driver in the middle, 106 built, and that long teardrop body feels like the future.

[图]

Next door, Pupil of Fate is brighter, with floor-to-ceiling glass and the cars spaced out like a gallery. The first thing I saw was a green Speedtail, a colour I'd never seen.

[图]

Then three McLaren Sennas, pale blue and black-and-white, plus a close-up of a tail. 500 built, named after the legendary driver, every detail made for the track.

[图]

[图]

The black Lamborghini Centenario, built for the founder's 100th birthday, the coupe limited to 40.

[图]

There are two more Valkyries here, grey with yellow lines, and next to the black one at First Motors each has its own beauty. It stopped me in my tracks again.

[图]

The AMG ONE shows up twice more here, and the one in the blue honeycomb livery is especially special.

[图]

A dark blue Bugatti Chiron with orange wheels, bold but really good looking.

[图]

Behind a glass door sits a quiet red Ferrari 550 Maranello, front V12 and a manual gearbox, the kind of old-school GT you can't buy new any more.

[图]

Last is the Ferrari Monza SP, no windscreen, retro styling, and SP1 and SP2 together total just 499.

[图]

Next up is fantasy time 🥹

stories.title: 塔什干，千禧年梦核？
stories.text:
从阿布扎比回莫斯科，中间在塔什干转机，空出来几个小时。没做任何攻略，出了机场就随便走走。

塔什干给我的第一感觉，是回到了国内的小县城。低矮的平房，路边的水渠，满街跑的是老款的小汽车和小面包车。下午的太阳斜斜地照下来，树下、草地上全是在玩的小孩；小超市里，孩子自己攥着钱，高高兴兴地买零食。物质条件说不上丰富，可每个人看起来都很热爱生活。

说不上来为什么，走在这里有一种千禧年梦核的感觉，像是小时候某个午后。惬意，舒适，还有一种很久没有过的安心。

乌兹别克斯坦和俄罗斯一样，曾经同属苏联，建筑和语言也有几分相似，可社会氛围和俄罗斯完全不同。

还有一件有意思的事：这里的人很喜欢韩国。市中心有一条首尔街，路上看到我，有人第一句话就是“你是韩国人吗？”

可一进到市中心，又是另一个世界。大商场、希尔顿、灯火通明的魔法城乐园，路上跑的是豪车，行人打扮得很时髦，和几公里外的平房、老车放在一起，像是两个时代。如果说外面是小县城，那这里就是县城中间圈出来的一座城，妥妥的村中城。
stories.textEn:
Flying from Abu Dhabi back to Moscow, I had a few hours to kill on a layover in Tashkent. No plans, no research; I just walked out of the airport and wandered.

My first impression was of a small county town back home in China. Low houses, irrigation ditches along the road, old cars and little vans everywhere. The afternoon sun came in low; kids were playing under every tree and on every patch of grass, and in the corner shops children clutched their own coins and happily bought snacks. Nobody here has much, but everyone seemed to love their life.

I can't quite say why, but walking around felt like Y2K dreamcore, like some afternoon from my childhood. Easy, comfortable, and a sense of safety I hadn't felt in a long time.

Uzbekistan, like Russia, was once part of the Soviet Union, and the buildings and language feel a little familiar, yet the mood of the place is nothing like Russia.

One more funny thing: people here love Korea. There is a Seoul Street in the city centre, and the first thing some people asked me was, "Are you Korean?"

Step into the centre, though, and you are in another world. Big malls, a Hilton, the blazing lights of the Magic City park, luxury cars on the road and people dressed in the latest fashion. Set against the low houses and old cars a few kilometres away, it feels like two different eras. If the outskirts are a county town, the centre is a city fenced off in the middle of it: a city inside a village.
