stories.title: 没说出口的谢谢
stories.titleEn: Tashkent, the thank-you we never said
stories.text:
在塔什干转机期间一共只待了几个小时。回头再想，街道和清真寺都已经模糊了，记住的全是人。

那天下午，我们一群人在景区门口转来转去，找不到吃饭的地方。语言不通，只好拦下一个小女孩，连比带划。她在景区里做导游，手上还有自己的活。

她听懂了，或者说，猜懂了。然后她没有随手指个方向了事，而是放下手里的活，先回趟家拿上东西，然后领着我们上了公交车。车票是她自己掏的钱，一路上谁也说不了几句话，我们就这么跟着她。到了餐厅门口，她转身就走了，头也没回。

没有等我们道谢，也没想要什么。好像把一群陌生的外国人送到饭馆，本来就是她这个下午该做的一件事，做完了，就回去接着干活。我们站在门口，那句憋了一路的谢谢，到最后也没能传达到。

那天还遇到另一个小导游：一个十六岁的男孩，会说七种语言。聊起来才知道，他的祖父是广东人。几代人之前从岭南出发的一条线，绕了大半个亚洲，落在塔什干街头这个少年身上，又在这个下午，和我们碰上了。

天黑以后去首尔街吃烧烤。那家小店那天刚开张，店里有个新疆人，是老板的熟人，特意跑来捧场。老板也自来熟，压根没把我们当外人。一间小店，几种语言，几拨原本不相干的人，热热闹闹地挤在一起，像谁家在办喜事。

最后是在机场。一位从名古屋来的老爷爷走过来，问我能不能借个充电器。

我们就这么聊了起来。他一把年纪，还在世界各地游历；话题几乎都是他起的头，一个接一个，聊得很开心。他身上有日本人的礼貌，却没有我印象里的那种拘谨，那种生怕给别人添麻烦的小心翼翼。主动找一个陌生人借东西、搭话，不太像一个传统的日本人会做的事。也许走过足够多的地方，人就会变成这样。

几个小时，几个人。他们大概不会记得我们，我们也没来得及好好说一声谢谢。那就写在这里吧。
stories.textEn:
I was only in Tashkent for a few hours. Looking back, the streets and the mosques have already blurred; what I remember clearly is the people.

That afternoon a group of us were circling outside a historic site, unable to find anywhere to eat. With no language in common, we stopped a girl and tried our best with gestures. She worked there as a guide and had her own work to do.

She understood, or rather, she guessed. And instead of just pointing us in a direction, she put down her work, took us onto a bus, and paid the fares herself. None of us could say much along the way; we simply followed her.

At the door of the restaurant she turned and left, without looking back.

She didn't wait to be thanked, and she didn't want anything. As if delivering a group of foreign strangers to a restaurant was simply one more thing she had to do that afternoon; done, and back to work. We stood at the door, and the thank-you we had been holding the whole way never made it across.

The kids on the street were the same. They didn't hide from the camera; they crowded in, striking poses for us to shoot.

That day we also met another young guide: a sixteen-year-old boy who speaks seven languages. Talking with him, we learned that his grandfather was from Guangdong. A thread that left southern China generations ago had wound across half of Asia, landed on a teenager on a street in Tashkent, and, that afternoon, crossed paths with ours.

After dark we went to Seoul Street for barbecue. The little place had opened that very day. A man from Xinjiang, a friend of the owner, had come by to show support, and the owner treated us as anything but outsiders. One small room, several languages, a few groups of people with nothing to do with each other, all squeezed in together, as noisy and warm as a family wedding.

And finally, the airport. An old man from Nagoya walked over and asked if he could borrow my charger.

That is how we started talking. At his age he is still travelling the world, and he was the one starting almost every topic, one after another; we had a great chat. He had the politeness I expect from Japanese people, but none of the stiffness, none of that careful fear of being a bother. Asking a stranger for something and striking up a conversation is not what a traditional Japanese person would usually do. Maybe that is what you become after travelling far enough.

A few hours, a few people. They probably won't remember us, and we never got to say thank you properly. So I'll write it here.

stories.title: 冬宫：一座宫殿装下的半部艺术史
stories.titleEn: The Winter Palace, room by room
stories.text:
冬宫这个名字其实有点“名不副实”：它既不只是一座宫殿，也不只在冬天好看。今天大家说的冬宫，指的是埃尔米塔日博物馆：冬宫本体，加上旁边的小埃尔米塔日、老埃尔米塔日、新埃尔米塔日和埃尔米塔日剧院，沿着涅瓦河连成一长排薄荷绿配白柱的建筑。

[图]

宫殿本身是伊丽莎白女皇请意大利建筑师拉斯特雷利盖的，1762 年完工，是沙皇在彼得堡的冬季居所。真正让它变成博物馆的是叶卡捷琳娜二世：1764 年她从柏林商人手里一口气买下两百多幅画，从此一发不可收拾，还专门在旁边加盖楼房来放这些东西。“埃尔米塔日”在法语里是“隐居处”的意思，原本是女皇和少数亲信躲起来看画的私人角落；直到 1852 年，新埃尔米塔日才第一次对公众开放。

1837 年冬宫还烧过一场大火，烧了好几天，大部分内装都是之后两年里照原样重建的。所以现在看到的金色天花和镶木地板，很多其实是 19 世纪中期的“复刻原版”。

现在馆藏大约三百万件。网上流行一个说法：每件看一分钟、每天看八小时，要看十几年，藏品含金量更是无需多言。所以要想一次看完，只能走马观花式的速通。那天勉强买到最后一个时段的门票，从下午四点多一直待到闭馆，走到腿软，下面是拍下来的一些房间和藏品。先放镇馆的三件：两幅达·芬奇，公认的达·芬奇真迹全世界也就十几二十幅，这里一口气有两幅；还有米开朗基罗的《蜷缩的男孩》，俄罗斯唯一一件他的雕塑。

[图]
stories.textEn:
The name is a little misleading: it isn't just one palace, and it isn't only worth seeing in winter. What people call the Winter Palace today is really the State Hermitage Museum: the palace itself plus the Small, Old and New Hermitage and the Hermitage Theatre, a long row of mint-green and white buildings along the Neva.

[图]

The palace was built for Empress Elizabeth by the Italian architect Rastrelli and finished in 1762 as the tsars' winter residence. The person who turned it into a museum was Catherine the Great. In 1764 she bought more than two hundred paintings from a Berlin merchant in one go, and from then on she simply couldn't stop, adding new buildings next door just to hold it all. "Hermitage" means a place of retreat in French: originally it was the private corner where the empress and a few close friends hid away with the pictures. The public was only let in when the New Hermitage opened in 1852.

In 1837 a fire gutted the palace for days, and most of the interiors were rebuilt to the old designs within two years. So a lot of the gilded ceilings and parquet floors you see are really mid-19th-century "faithful originals".

The collection now runs to around three million objects. There's a popular claim that if you spent one minute on each, eight hours a day, it would take you more than a decade. So don't try to see it all; pick a few halls and take your time. I stayed from a bit after four until closing and walked until my legs gave out. These are some of the rooms and pieces I photographed. First, the three highlights: two paintings by Leonardo da Vinci (only around fifteen to twenty are generally accepted as his, and the Hermitage has two of them), and Michelangelo's Crouching Boy, the only sculpture by him in Russia.

[图]

media.caption: 从圣以撒大教堂柱廊往北看：金色尖顶是海军部，河对岸是彼得保罗要塞，右边那一长排就是冬宫
达·芬奇《哺乳圣母》（《利塔圣母》），约 1490 年。名字来自曾收藏它的米兰利塔家族，1865 年卖给了沙皇
达·芬奇《持花圣母》（《伯努瓦圣母》），他二十多岁时的早期作品，1914 年从伯努瓦家族买来。存世的达·芬奇画作不到二十幅，这里有两幅
米开朗基罗《蜷缩的男孩》，据说原本是为美第奇家族礼拜堂准备的，俄罗斯唯一一件米开朗基罗的雕塑
拉斐尔长廊。叶卡捷琳娜二世看了梵蒂冈拉斐尔长廊的画稿念念不忘，干脆让人在彼得堡原样复制了一条，拱顶每一格都是手绘
亭阁厅，19 世纪中期斯塔肯施奈德设计，摩尔式拱、哥特式线条和文艺复兴柱子混在一起，挂了二十多盏水晶吊灯
孔雀钟，英国工匠詹姆斯·考克斯 18 世纪做的机械钟，波将金买来送给叶卡捷琳娜二世。运转时孔雀开屏、猫头鹰转头、公鸡打鸣，至今还能走（网上有“被乾隆退货”的说法，考克斯确实给中国做过不少机械钟，但这台并没有可靠记载，看个乐就好）
夜里的长廊，吊灯一盏接一盏延伸到尽头
雕塑长廊，古典雕像沿着彩绘拱顶一路排开
意大利绘画厅的红墙和巨大的镀金烛台，人站旁边才显出它有多高
窗上嵌着的彩色玻璃，透过它能看到外面的冬天
提香《基督祝福》，晚年作品，手里托着象征世界的水晶球
提香《忏悔的抹大拉的玛利亚》，同一题材提香画过好几版，这是晚年那版，笔触更松、情绪更浓。外面那圈雕满人像的画框本身也是件艺术品
朱利奥·罗马诺《恋人》，约 1525 年。注意右边门口有个老妇人在偷看，这位拉斐尔的得意弟子很会讲故事
卢卡·焦尔达诺《拉皮斯人与半人马之战》，婚礼上喝醉的半人马抢新娘，画面挤满了扭打的人和马
卡洛·多尔奇《圣塞西莉亚》，音乐的守护圣人，那片蓝色是整幅画最抢眼的地方
瓦伦丁·德·布伦《驱逐圣殿里的商贩》，卡拉瓦乔式的强烈明暗，翻倒的桌子和惊慌的人定格在一瞬间
伦勃朗《以撒献祭》，1635 年。天使抓住亚伯拉罕的手，刀正从半空掉下来
伦勃朗《浪子回头》，晚年作品，冬宫最出名的画之一。父亲把手搭在跪着的儿子背上，整幅画安静得像在呼吸
伦勃朗《达娜厄》，1636 年。1985 年有人朝它泼硫酸、还捅了两刀，修复了十二年才重新挂出来
伦勃朗晚年的《哈曼认命》（也有人认为画的是大卫与乌利亚），红袍人物低着头，说不清是悲伤还是认命
弗兰斯·斯奈德斯《鸟的音乐会》，猫头鹰捧着乐谱当指挥，周围的鸟都张着嘴在唱
迪克·雅各布斯《阿姆斯特丹射手连队群像》，1530 年代，十几个男人挤在一个画框里，荷兰群像画早期的样子
菲利普·德·尚帕涅《摩西与十诫》，摩西捧着石板，头上冒出两撮光
尼古拉斯·贝尔赫姆《劫掠欧罗巴》，宙斯变成白牛把公主驮走
庚斯博罗《穿蓝衣的女士》，冬宫英国绘画里最受欢迎的一幅，灰蓝色的衣裙和蓬松的发髻特别 18 世纪
戈弗雷·内勒《约翰·洛克像》，1697 年，就是写《政府论》的那位哲学家
约瑟夫·赖特《圣天使堡的烟火》，罗马的烟火表演把夜空照成一片橘红
还是约瑟夫·赖特，《铁匠铺》。他最擅长画烛光、炉火这类黑暗里的光
雷诺兹《丘比特解开维纳斯的腰带》，雷诺兹给波将金画过好几幅画，后来都进了冬宫
托马斯·劳伦斯《沃龙佐娃伯爵夫人像》，这位伯爵夫人据说是普希金暗恋过的人
罗蒙诺索夫工坊做的彼得大帝马赛克像，18 世纪中期，远看像油画，近看是一粒粒彩色玻璃
维热-勒布伦《亚历山德拉和叶连娜两位女大公》，叶卡捷琳娜二世的两个孙女，据说女皇一开始嫌画得太随意
瓦西里·季姆画的 1825 年 12 月 14 日枢密院广场，十二月党人起义那天
镀金雪橇，前头雕着骑马的人，宫廷冬天出游用的
骑士大厅里的全身盔甲
披着鳞片马甲的东方骑兵
清代官员像，补服、朝珠、顶戴都画得一丝不苟
一对穿红袍的夫妇像，古代中国祖先像的样式
中国瓷器，红彩的鱼和龙在白瓷上游
一整面墙的中国墨锭，各种形状和描金纹样摆成了图案
日本书法「東天紅」，要从右往左读，意思是东边天空泛红、天快亮了，落款是昭和年间
巴泽雷克毛毡挂毯局部，阿尔泰山古墓出土，两千多年前的骑马人颜色还在
古罗马石棺，盖子上躺着墓主人的雕像

stories.title: 一个商人买下的俄罗斯画史
stories.titleEn: The Tretyakov, one merchant's history of Russian art
stories.text:
特列季亚科夫画廊藏在莫斯科河南岸的扎莫斯克沃列奇耶，一片安静的老街区里。从克里姆林宫过河走十几分钟，拐进拉夫鲁申斯基胡同，就能看到那座红白相间、像从童话书里搬出来的小楼。

[图]

它的来头很朴素：一个商人的私人收藏。巴维尔·特列季亚科夫是做纺织生意的，1856 年开始买画，而且专买同时代的俄罗斯画家。那时候俄国上流社会眼里只有欧洲大师，本土画家卖画难，特列季亚科夫就成了他们最靠得住的买家，很多后来进了教科书的画，当年都是他第一个掏钱。1892 年，他把自己和弟弟谢尔盖的收藏一起捐给了莫斯科市，这才有了今天的国立特列季亚科夫画廊。

现在的正门立面是画家瓦斯涅佐夫在 1900 年代初设计的，用的是古罗斯的木结构和装饰纹样，在一排排普通公寓楼中间特别显眼。主楼只讲俄罗斯艺术，从古代圣像一路排到 20 世纪初，按时间走一圈，差不多就是一部俄罗斯绘画史；更晚的先锋派和苏联艺术在克里米亚堤岸那边的新馆。

和冬宫比，这里没那么金碧辉煌，墙是安静的灰绿色，人也少一些，能凑近慢慢看。很多画在国内课本、画册里见过，真站到跟前，尺寸和颜色都跟印象里不太一样。先放两幅最想看的：列宾的《伊凡雷帝杀子》，真站在它面前比想象中还要压抑，沙皇瞪大的眼睛、地毯上的血，隔着护栏和玻璃都让人后背发凉；还有克拉姆斯柯依的《无名女郎》，在国内的名气大概比这座画廊本身还大。后面再按参观的顺序，放一些印象深的。

[图]

[图]
stories.textEn:
The Tretyakov Gallery sits south of the Moscow River in Zamoskvorechye, a quiet old neighbourhood. Cross the river from the Kremlin, walk for ten minutes or so, turn into Lavrushinsky Lane, and there it is: a red-and-white building that looks like it stepped out of a book of fairy tales.

[图]

Its origins are modest: one merchant's private collection. Pavel Tretyakov made his money in textiles and started buying paintings in 1856, and he only bought living Russian artists. Back then high society only cared about the European masters, and Russian painters struggled to sell. Tretyakov became the buyer they could count on, and a lot of pictures that ended up in textbooks were first paid for by him. In 1892 he gave his collection, together with his brother Sergei's, to the city of Moscow, and that is how the State Tretyakov Gallery began.

The facade you see today was designed by the painter Viktor Vasnetsov in the early 1900s, borrowing the shapes and ornament of old Russian wooden architecture. Among the ordinary apartment blocks around it, it really stands out. The main building is all Russian art, from medieval icons to the early 20th century, so walking through it in order is more or less a history of Russian painting. The later avant-garde and Soviet art live in the New Tretyakov on Krymsky Val.

Compared with the Hermitage it is less dazzling: grey-green walls, fewer people, and you can get close and take your time. Many of these paintings I had only seen as small reproductions, and in front of the real thing the size and the colours were never quite what I expected. First, the two I most wanted to see. Repin's Ivan the Terrible and His Son Ivan is even heavier in person than I imagined: the tsar's wide eyes, the blood on the carpet; even behind the railing and the glass it sends a chill down your back. And Kramskoi's Unknown Woman, which in China is probably more famous than the gallery itself. After that, the rest in the order I saw them.

[图]

[图]

media.caption: 正门。瓦斯涅佐夫设计的立面像一座古罗斯木头楼阁，正中嵌着莫斯科城徽上的圣乔治屠龙浮雕
进门先上一段铺红毯的楼梯，展厅从二楼的 18 世纪开始
列宾《伊凡雷帝杀子》，1885 年。暴怒的沙皇失手打死儿子，抱着他瞪大眼睛。这幅画先后两次被人袭击，1913 年被划了刀，2018 年又被人用金属杆砸坏玻璃，现在前面隔着护栏
克拉姆斯柯依《无名女郎》，1883 年。国内很多人认识这幅，但画上到底是谁，一百多年了也没人说得清
列维茨基《叶卡捷琳娜二世：正义女神神庙里的立法者》。女皇往祭坛上烧罂粟花，罂粟代表睡眠，意思是为了国家牺牲自己的安宁，很典型的宫廷宣传画
伊万·阿尔古诺夫《垂死的克娄巴特拉》，1750 年。阿尔古诺夫是舍列梅捷夫伯爵家的农奴画家，胸口那条小蛇就是故事的结局
费奥多尔·阿列克谢耶夫《莫斯科红场》，1801 年。他被叫作“俄国的卡纳莱托”，两百多年前的红场，瓦西里升天大教堂和斯帕斯塔都还认得出来
还是阿列克谢耶夫，《从彼得保罗要塞看宫廷沿岸街》，1794 年。对岸那一排里就有冬宫，和上一篇正好呼应
基普连斯基《戴罂粟花环的女孩》，1819 年在意大利画的。小姑娘的眼神有点警惕，不太像在乖乖当模特
基普连斯基《茹科夫斯基像》，1816 年。茹科夫斯基是诗人，也是普希金的前辈和朋友，背后阴沉的天和废墟是浪漫主义的标配
亚历山大·伊万诺夫《基督显现于民众》。画了二十年，宽七米多，画廊专门给它留了一个厅，站远了才看得全
普基廖夫《不相称的婚姻》，1862 年。年迈的官员娶年轻的新娘，新娘眼睛都哭红了。传说右边抱着胳膊瞪着他们的年轻人，就是画家本人
弗拉维茨基《塔拉卡诺娃公主》，1864 年。传说这个自称女皇之女的女人被关在彼得保罗要塞，大水灌进牢房，老鼠往床上爬。其实她在洪水前就病死了，但这个版本流传最广
费奥多尔·瓦西里耶夫《解冻》，1871 年。画这幅的时候他才二十一岁，两年后就死于肺结核。灰蒙蒙的一片，越看越冷
艾瓦佐夫斯基《彩虹》，1873 年。他一辈子画了六千多幅海，这幅一反常态，几乎全是浅色，彩虹淡到要找一下
弗鲁贝尔厅里的釉陶面具。弗鲁贝尔在阿布拉姆采沃的陶瓷作坊里做过不少这种东西，卷曲的头发像海浪
弗鲁贝尔《梦幻公主》，1896 年为下诺夫哥罗德博览会画的大幅装饰画，当年被评委会拒收，现在一整面墙都是它
弗鲁贝尔的《浮士德》三联画，1896 年给莫斯科一位富商宅邸里的哥特式书房画的
列宾《亚历山大三世在彼得罗夫宫庭院接见乡长》，1886 年。一院子的农民代表，表情各不相同，是列宾很擅长的群像
苏里科夫《近卫军临刑的早晨》，1881 年。1698 年近卫军叛乱后，彼得大帝在红场处决叛军，右边骑马的就是彼得。整幅画没有画行刑，只画了行刑前的那一刻
苏里科夫《缅希科夫在别廖佐沃》，1883 年。彼得大帝的头号宠臣失势后被流放西伯利亚，一家人挤在小木屋里。有人说要是缅希科夫站起来，头会撞到天花板
韦列夏金《帖木儿的门》，1872 年。雕花大门前站着两个守卫，背对着我们，门里是什么谁也看不到
韦列夏金《战败者·安魂祭》，1878–1879 年。俄土战争后，神父在一片铺满阵亡士兵的荒原上做祷告。韦列夏金自己上过战场，最后也死在战舰上
瓦斯涅佐夫《伊万王子骑灰狼》，1889 年。俄罗斯童话里的经典场景，画家就是设计画廊正门的那位
希施金《橡树林中的雨》，1891 年。希施金以画森林出名，这幅里的雨雾把远处的人和树都化开了
安托科尔斯基的大理石雕像《伊凡雷帝》。和列宾那幅放在一起看，是同一个沙皇的两种样子
雅罗申科《处处有生活》，1888 年。囚车的铁窗后面，一家人在给站台上的鸽子撒面包屑
克拉姆斯柯依《月夜》，1880 年。白衣女子坐在夜里的长椅上，整幅画都是凉凉的月光
克拉姆斯柯依《荒野中的基督》，1872 年。没有光环、没有神迹，就是一个人坐在石头上想事情
克拉姆斯柯依《五月之夜（美人鱼）》，1871 年，取材于果戈理的小说，月光下的水边坐着一群溺水姑娘变成的美人鱼
《非人手所造的救主》，12 世纪诺夫哥罗德的圣像，是馆里最古老的一批藏品之一，单独放在暗处的玻璃柜里
布拉兹《契诃夫像》，1898 年。契诃夫本人不太喜欢，说自己在画里的表情像刚闻了辣根
出门后旁边的新楼，外墙上印着馆藏画作的放大复制，看着像是彼得罗夫-沃德金的《浴红马》

stories.title: 圣彼得堡：一座用意志造出来的城
stories.titleEn: Saint Petersburg, a city built on will
stories.text:
在俄罗斯这一年多，去过不少城市，最喜欢的始终是圣彼得堡。一月和七月各去了一趟：一次大雪，白天短得只剩六个小时；一次白夜，太阳落下去没多久就又升起来。同一座城，两副面孔，底下是同一个灵魂。

[图]

一　沼泽上的意志

圣彼得堡不是自然长出来的城市，是一个人硬生生“想”出来的。1703 年 5 月，北方战争打到第三年，彼得一世刚从瑞典人手里夺下涅瓦河口，就在河口一座叫兔子岛的小岛上动工修建要塞，也就是今天的彼得保罗要塞，这一天被算作这座城的生日。那里原本是芬兰湾尽头的一片沼泽，地势低洼，常年潮湿，冬天封冻，秋天发洪水，任何一个正常的君主都不会把城建在这儿。但彼得要的就是这片水：俄罗斯没有一个像样的、通向欧洲的出海口，他要在这里造船、建海军，用后来普希金的话说，“打开一扇通向欧洲的窗”。

[图]

代价是惊人的。成千上万的农奴、士兵和瑞典战俘被征调过来，在泥水里打桩、挖渠、填地，死于寒冷、疾病和劳累的人不计其数，民间一直有“这座城建在白骨上”的说法。为了让城快点立起来，彼得下令全国其他地方一律不准盖石头房子，石匠只能来彼得堡干活；进城的大车和船只还得按规定捎上几块石头，算是“入城税”。1712 年前后，他干脆把首都从莫斯科迁了过来，逼着贵族们搬家、剃胡子、穿欧式衣服、学跳舞。圣彼得堡从诞生那天起，就是一座带着强烈意志的城市：它不顺应自然，而是和自然、和旧俄罗斯对着干。

[图]

1709 年波尔塔瓦一战，彼得大败瑞典国王卡尔十二世，北方战争的胜负从此定了下来。1735 年，为了纪念这场大胜，城西彼得霍夫夏宫的大瀑布中央立起了一尊镀金的参孙像，参孙双手撕开狮子的嘴：狮子是瑞典国徽上的动物，而波尔塔瓦会战那天正好是圣参孙节。彼得霍夫常被叫作“俄罗斯的凡尔赛”，宫殿正对着芬兰湾，彼得当年就在这里看他的舰队。二战时德军占领了这里，宫殿被烧成空壳，参孙像也不知所踪，今天看到的几乎都是战后一点点照原样复原的。冬天喷泉全部停了，园子里只剩下雪，金色的雕像在一片白里反倒更亮。

[图]

[图]

此后两百年，彼得堡一直是俄罗斯帝国的首都，也是一座革命的城市。1825 年十二月党人在枢密院广场起事；1881 年亚历山大二世在运河边被炸身亡；1905 年请愿的工人在冬宫前被枪杀，史称“流血星期日”；1917 年，二月革命推翻了沙皇，十月里阿芙乐尔号巡洋舰的一声空炮，成了攻打冬宫的信号。城市的名字也跟着时代换了好几次：一战时嫌“堡”字太像德语，改叫彼得格勒；1924 年列宁去世，改叫列宁格勒；1991 年市民投票，又改回圣彼得堡。不过本地人最常挂在嘴边的，还是那个亲昵的简称：“皮特”。

[图]

二　列宁格勒的 872 天

1941 年 9 月 8 日，德军攻占了拉多加湖边的什利谢利堡，列宁格勒和外界的陆路联系被彻底切断。围困从那天开始，一直到 1944 年 1 月 27 日才完全解除，整整 872 天。希特勒的打算不是攻进城，而是把它围死，让这座城连同城里的人一起从地图上消失。

第一个冬天最难熬。没有暖气，没有电，没有自来水，气温跌到零下三十度。1941 年 11 月下旬，面包配给降到最低点：工人每天 250 克，职员、家属和孩子只有 125 克，而那块“面包”里还掺着大量纤维素、麸皮和别的东西。人们煮皮带，刮墙纸上的浆糊，街上不时有人倒下就再也没起来，用雪橇拖着裹布的遗体去墓地，是那年冬天最常见的画面。十一岁的女孩塔尼娅·萨维切娃在一个小本子上，一页一页记下家人去世的日期，最后几页只写着：萨维切夫一家死了，全都死了，只剩下塔尼娅一个。她后来被疏散出城，但也没能活下来。围困期间死去的平民，各方估计从六十多万到一百多万不等，绝大多数死于饥饿。

维系这座城的，是冰上的“生命之路”：拉多加湖封冻以后，卡车冒着炮火和随时可能裂开的冰面，把粮食运进来，把老人和孩子运出去。而让这座城在精神上没有垮掉的，是一些今天听起来近乎不可思议的事。城里的广播几乎从没断过，没有节目的时候，喇叭里就放节拍器的声音，告诉大家城市还活着；诗人奥莉加·别尔戈利茨每天在电台里念诗。冬宫的工作人员把一百多万件藏品疏散到乌拉尔，自己留下来住在地下室，守着一屋子空画框，据说还给前线来的士兵对着空画框“讲解”上面原本挂着什么画。1942 年 8 月 9 日，肖斯塔科维奇的《第七交响曲》在被围困的城里演出，乐团是临时拼凑的，有乐手在排练期间饿死，演出通过扩音器对着德军阵地播放。据说多年以后，一位当年的德国士兵说，听到音乐的那一刻，他就知道这座城是拿不下了。

[图]

1945 年，列宁格勒成为第一批被称作“英雄城市”的城市。今天起义广场边那栋酒店的楼顶，每晚还亮着“英雄城市列宁格勒”几个大字；涅瓦大街 14 号的墙上，保留着当年的白底蓝字：“公民们！炮击时，街道这一侧最危险。”城北的皮斯卡廖夫公墓里，埋着约五十万围城死难者，纪念墙上刻着别尔戈利茨的诗句：“谁也没有被忘记，什么也没有被忘记。”每年 1 月 27 日，总有人去那里献花，有人还会放下一小块黑面包。

[图]

要理解圣彼得堡人，得先理解这 872 天。这座城挨过饿，失去了上百万人，却始终没有投降，也没有放弃那些“没用”的东西：诗、音乐、博物馆、体面。我觉得这就是这座城的精神内核，一种骄傲的、近乎固执的尊严。帝国的辉煌是它的外衣，这份在废墟里也要守住的东西，才是它的骨头。

三　圣彼得堡人

莫斯科人和彼得堡人互相看不顺眼是出了名的。俄罗斯有一大堆关于两座城的段子：同一样东西两边叫法都不一样，路缘石莫斯科叫 бордюр，彼得堡偏叫 поребрик；楼门洞莫斯科叫 подъезд，彼得堡叫 парадная；连街边的卷饼，一边叫 шаурма，一边叫 шаверма。有句老话说，莫斯科是俄罗斯的心脏，彼得堡是俄罗斯的头脑。莫斯科人嫌彼得堡人清高、慢吞吞、穷讲究；彼得堡人嫌莫斯科人眼里只有钱、太浮躁。彼得堡人很乐意把自己的城叫作“文化首都”，说话慢条斯理，用词考究，连排队都比莫斯科从容。

我的感受是，彼得堡人身上有一种很特别的自由。这种自由不张扬，是一种“我就这样”的松弛：穿什么都行，留什么头发都行，在河堤上坐一整晚也行，没人多看你一眼。街头艺人比莫斯科多得多，涅瓦大街上拉琴的、弹吉他的、敲木琴的、唱摇滚的，从下午一直演到后半夜。这里也是苏联摇滚的老家：1981 年列宁格勒摇滚俱乐部成立，“电影”乐队的维克多·崔、“水族馆”的格列本希科夫都是从这座城走出去的，崔还在一间叫“堪察加”的锅炉房里当过锅炉工，一边烧锅炉一边写歌。直到今天，这里的年轻人还是比别处更爱地下音乐、独立书店、老房子里的小酒吧和屋顶。

[图]

[图]

夏天的彼得堡是另一个世界。五月底到七月中是白夜，最亮的六月下旬，太阳晚上十点多才落，凌晨三点多又升起来，中间那几个小时天也不会真正黑下去，只是变成一种淡淡的蓝。整座城像是集体失眠：半夜十二点，河堤上坐满了人，喝酒的、弹琴的、接吻的，游船一艘接一艘从桥下穿过。凌晨一点多，涅瓦河上的桥一座接一座升起来给货船让路，岸边挤满了等着看开桥的人，桥面立起来的那一刻掌声和欢呼声一片；错过最后一班桥的人，就只能在对岸等到天亮。六月底还有“红帆节”，一艘挂着红帆的船在烟花里驶过涅瓦河，给中学毕业生庆祝。

[图]

[图]

七月那趟，正赶上午夜的宫廷桥白夜马拉松。几千人从涅瓦河边、从冬宫前跑过，路灯开着，天却没黑，路边的人喊着加油，跑者冲着镜头挥手、张开双臂，像过节一样。那几天我几乎没怎么睡，天一直亮着，总觉得睡觉是一种浪费。

[图]

[图]

白天去城西的芬兰湾边，又是另一种安静。有人赤脚走进凉凉的海水，有人在礁石上一坐就是一整个傍晚，沙滩上的石头被人一块块垒成小塔。波罗的海的水是灰蓝色的，不算好看，但很安静。

[图]

冬天则完全反过来。十二月最短的时候，白天不到六个小时，上午十点天才亮，下午四点就黑了，大多数日子天空是一整片灰。一月那趟正好赶上东正教圣诞节，大雪下了好几天，芬兰湾冻成了一望无际的冰原，有人支着小马扎在冰上凿洞钓鱼，有人就那么一个人慢慢走向白茫茫的中央。孩子们在雪地里打滚，大狗跟着一起疯；教堂里挤满来做圣诞礼拜的人，烛光一片。冬天的彼得堡是安静的、向内的，也是最“彼得堡”的。

[图]

[图]

[图]

彼得堡常被说成是俄罗斯最“欧洲”的城市，这话不假。街道的尺度、运河、咖啡馆、讲究的年轻人、对艺术和个人空间的尊重，都让人恍惚觉得是在阿姆斯特丹或者巴黎。但待久了会发现，它和西欧终究不一样。这里的天太低，冬天太长，历史太重。普希金写过在洪水里失去一切、最后发了疯的小职员，果戈里写过丢了外套就郁郁而终的小人物，陀思妥耶夫斯基让他的主人公在干草广场边的阁楼里发着高烧，还说这是全世界最抽象、最“蓄意”的城市。彼得堡人身上有一抹很淡的悲情：热闹的时候也带着一点清醒，狂欢的时候也知道狂欢会结束。白夜之所以疯得那么彻底，大概正是因为每个人都记得，冬天很快就会回来。

[图]

诗人布罗茨基被苏联驱逐出境，到死也没再回来，年轻时却写过：不选国家也不选墓地，要回瓦西里岛去死。很多彼得堡人对这座城的感情大概就是这样：抱怨它的天气、它的潮湿、它的不如意，但它是唯一的那一个。

[图]

四　石头写成的城

彼得堡是一座规划出来的城市。它没有莫斯科那种一圈套一圈、层层叠加的混乱，街道笔直，广场开阔，建筑沿着河岸整整齐齐地排开。彼得请来了意大利、法国、德国的建筑师，此后两百年里，特雷齐尼、拉斯特雷利、夸伦吉、罗西、蒙费朗……一代代人在这里把巴洛克、古典主义和帝国风格做到了极致。罗西设计的那条街，宽 22 米，两边楼高 22 米，长 220 米，比例严丝合缝。更关键的是，1844 年起城里有一条执行得很严的规矩：民用建筑不能高过冬宫。于是整座城的天际线几乎是平的，只有教堂的穹顶和海军部、彼得保罗大教堂的金色尖顶刺出来，站在高处看，像一片安静的石头海。

[图]

圣以撒大教堂是这片石头海里最大的那块。法国建筑师蒙费朗为它花了整整 40 年（1818—1858），一百多根整块花岗岩的柱子是从芬兰湾对岸的采石场运来的，金顶据说用掉了一百多公斤黄金。苏联时期它当过“无神论博物馆”，穹顶下还挂过傅科摆。爬上柱廊，整个市中心都在脚下：海军部的金针、冬宫、彼得保罗要塞，还有远处海边的拉赫塔中心。

[图]

和周围的欧式建筑格格不入的，是滴血救世主教堂。1881 年，亚历山大二世在格里博耶多夫运河边被民意党人的炸弹炸成重伤，当天就去世了，他的儿子在遇刺的地方盖起这座教堂，用的是莫斯科式的洋葱顶和彩砖。里面几乎每一寸墙面都是马赛克，加起来有七千多平方米。冬天傍晚亮灯以后，它在雪里像一则童话。

[图]

涅瓦大街是城市的主轴，一头是海军部，一头是亚历山大·涅夫斯基修道院。喀山大教堂仿照罗马圣彼得大教堂修了一道半圆形的柱廊，打败拿破仑的统帅库图佐夫就葬在里面；斜对面的胜家大楼，楼顶托着一只玻璃地球仪，原本是美国胜家缝纫机公司的办公楼，现在是城里最有名的书店“百年书屋”。新年前后，整条大街挂满了灯，从高处往下看，是一条发光的河。

[图]

[图]

再往城里走，有蓝色穹顶上撒满金星的伊兹梅洛夫斯基圣三一大教堂，有拉斯特雷利设计的蓝白色斯莫尔尼大教堂，还有运河上一座接一座的小桥，“北方威尼斯”的名字不是白叫的。格里博耶多夫运河一路弯到干草广场，那里就是《罪与罚》的地盘：拉斯柯尔尼科夫从他的阁楼走到放高利贷的老太婆家，书里写着，不多不少七百三十步。

[图]

艺术在这里不是装饰，是空气。冬宫里有三百万件藏品，俄罗斯博物馆里挂着列宾和艾瓦佐夫斯基，马林斯基剧院首演过《睡美人》和《胡桃夹子》。普希金、果戈里、陀思妥耶夫斯基、阿赫玛托娃、纳博科夫、布罗茨基，柴可夫斯基、里姆斯基-科萨科夫、肖斯塔科维奇……俄罗斯文化史上差不多一半的名字，都和这座城连在一起。

[图]

七月那趟我去了涅瓦大街尽头的亚历山大·涅夫斯基修道院，墓园里走一圈就是一部人物志，陀思妥耶夫斯基、柴可夫斯基、穆索尔斯基都葬在这里。我在一块花岗岩墓前停下，牌子上写着“Л. ЭЙЛЕР 1707—1783”，是数学家欧拉，他前后在彼得堡科学院工作了三十多年，最后也在这里去世。不远处还有一块刻着汉字的墓碑，是俄国汉学的奠基人比丘林，也就是雅金甫神父，他在北京住了十几年，把很多中国典籍第一次译成俄文。在俄罗斯的墓园里读到“無時勤勞 垂光史冊”八个字，感觉很奇妙。

[图]

唯一冲破这条天际线的，是 2019 年建成的拉赫塔中心，462 米，欧洲最高楼。它原本打算盖在市中心对岸，因为会破坏历史天际线，被市民和联合国教科文组织一路反对，最后只好挪到城市西北的海边。我挺喜欢这个结局：这座城愿意接纳新的东西，前提是别碰它的老规矩。

[图]

说到底，圣彼得堡是一座“本不该存在”的城市：建在沼泽上，冬天漫长又黑暗，被围困到几乎死绝，却一直站在那里，美得那么用力。它有欧洲的骨架，俄罗斯的灵魂，还有一种只属于它自己的、带着悲伤的骄傲。每次离开，我都觉得自己还会回来。

[图]
stories.textEn:
In more than a year in Russia I have been to a lot of cities, and Saint Petersburg is still my favourite. I went once in January and once in July: one trip buried in snow, with barely six hours of daylight; the other in the white nights, when the sun goes down and is back up again almost before you notice. Same city, two faces, one soul underneath. I want to write about it properly: first where it came from, then the people who live there, and finally its buildings and its art.

[图]

I. Willpower on a swamp

Saint Petersburg did not grow on its own. One man willed it into existence. In May 1703, three years into the Great Northern War, Peter I had just taken the mouth of the Neva from the Swedes, and he began building a fortress on a small island there called Hare Island. That fortress is today's Peter and Paul Fortress, and that day counts as the city's birthday. The place was a swamp at the far end of the Gulf of Finland: low, wet all year, frozen in winter, flooded in autumn. No sensible ruler would have put a city there. But the water was exactly what Peter wanted. Russia had no proper sea gate to Europe, so he would build ships and a navy here, and, as Pushkin later put it, cut a window through to Europe.

[图]

The cost was staggering. Tens of thousands of serfs, soldiers and Swedish prisoners of war were brought in to drive piles, dig canals and fill land in the mud. Countless people died of cold, disease and exhaustion, and people still say the city was built on bones. To get it up faster, Peter banned stone construction everywhere else in the country, so stonemasons had nowhere to work but Petersburg, and every cart and ship entering the city had to bring a few stones as a kind of entry tax. Around 1712 he simply moved the capital here from Moscow and made the nobility relocate, shave their beards, dress like Europeans and learn to dance. From its first day, Petersburg was a city of sheer will: it did not adapt to nature, it fought against nature and against old Russia.

[图]

In 1709, at Poltava, Peter crushed Charles XII of Sweden, and the war was effectively decided. In 1735, to mark the victory, a gilded Samson tearing open a lion's jaws was set up in the middle of the Grand Cascade at Peterhof, west of the city. The lion was the beast on the Swedish coat of arms, and the battle of Poltava had fallen on St Samson's day. Peterhof is often called the Russian Versailles. The palace faces the Gulf of Finland, and Peter used to watch his fleet from here. In the Second World War the Germans occupied it, the palace was burnt to a shell and the Samson vanished; almost everything you see today was painstakingly rebuilt after the war. In winter the fountains are all switched off, the gardens are nothing but snow, and the gold statues shine even brighter against all that white.

[图]

[图]

For the next two hundred years Petersburg was the capital of the Russian Empire, and it was also a city of revolutions. In 1825 the Decembrists rose on Senate Square. In 1881 Alexander II was killed by a bomb beside a canal. In 1905 petitioning workers were shot in front of the Winter Palace, the day remembered as Bloody Sunday. In 1917 the February Revolution brought down the tsar, and in October a blank shot from the cruiser Aurora became the signal to storm the Winter Palace. The city's name changed with the times: during the First World War "-burg" sounded too German, so it became Petrograd; after Lenin died in 1924 it became Leningrad; in 1991 residents voted and it went back to Saint Petersburg. Locals, though, mostly just call it by its fond short name, "Piter".

[图]

II. Leningrad's 872 days

On 8 September 1941 German troops took Shlisselburg on Lake Ladoga, and Leningrad's land links with the rest of the country were cut. The siege that began that day was not fully lifted until 27 January 1944: 872 days. Hitler's plan was not to storm the city but to starve it, to wipe it off the map together with everyone in it.

The first winter was the worst. No heating, no electricity, no running water, and temperatures down to minus thirty. In late November 1941 the bread ration hit its lowest point: 250 grams a day for workers, and just 125 grams for office staff, dependants and children, and that "bread" was padded out with cellulose, bran and whatever else could be found. People boiled leather belts and scraped the paste off wallpaper. People fell in the street and never got up, and sledges dragging bodies wrapped in cloth to the cemetery were the commonest sight that winter. An eleven-year-old girl, Tanya Savicheva, wrote down in a small notebook the date each member of her family died, page after page. The last pages say only: the Savichevs are dead, they are all dead, only Tanya is left. She was later evacuated, but she did not survive either. Estimates of civilian deaths in the siege range from over six hundred thousand to more than a million, most of them from hunger.

What kept the city alive was the Road of Life across the ice: once Lake Ladoga froze, trucks drove across it under shellfire, on ice that could crack at any moment, bringing food in and taking the old and the young out. What kept the city from breaking in spirit were things that sound almost unbelievable today. The city radio hardly ever went silent; when there was nothing to broadcast, the loudspeakers played a metronome, to let people know the city was still alive. The poet Olga Berggolts read poems on the radio every day. Hermitage staff sent more than a million objects away to the Urals and stayed behind themselves, living in the basements and guarding rooms of empty frames; it is said they even gave soldiers from the front "tours" of the empty frames, describing the paintings that used to hang in them. On 9 August 1942 Shostakovich's Seventh Symphony was performed in the besieged city by a scratch orchestra, some of whose musicians starved to death during rehearsals, and it was broadcast through loudspeakers towards the German lines. Years later, so the story goes, a former German soldier said that the moment he heard the music he knew the city could not be taken.

[图]

In 1945 Leningrad was among the first cities to be called a Hero City. Today the words "Hero City Leningrad" still light up every night on the roof of the hotel on Vosstaniya Square, and on the wall of 14 Nevsky Prospekt the old blue-on-white sign is still there: "Citizens! During shelling this side of the street is the most dangerous." At Piskaryovskoye Cemetery in the north of the city lie around half a million victims of the siege, and the memorial wall carries Berggolts's line: "No one is forgotten, nothing is forgotten." Every year on 27 January people come with flowers, and some leave a small piece of black bread.

[图]

To understand the people of Petersburg you have to understand those 872 days. The city starved and lost more than a million people, yet it never surrendered, and it never gave up the "useless" things: poetry, music, museums, dignity. That, to me, is the core of the city: a proud, almost stubborn dignity. The splendour of empire is its coat; this thing it held on to even in ruins is its bones.

III. The people of Petersburg

Muscovites and Petersburgers famously get on each other's nerves. Russia is full of jokes about the two cities. The same thing has a different name in each: a kerb is бордюр in Moscow and поребрик in Petersburg; a building entrance is подъезд in Moscow and парадная in Petersburg; even the street wrap is шаурма in one and шаверма in the other. An old saying goes that Moscow is Russia's heart and Petersburg is its head. Muscovites find Petersburgers aloof, slow and fussy; Petersburgers find Muscovites money-obsessed and restless. Petersburgers like to call their city the "cultural capital". They speak slowly, choose their words with care, and even queue more calmly than Moscow does.

What I feel in Petersburgers is a very particular kind of freedom. It is not loud; it is a relaxed "this is just how I am". Wear whatever you like, grow your hair however you like, sit on the embankment all night, and nobody looks twice. There are far more street musicians than in Moscow: violins, guitars, a xylophone, rock bands, playing along Nevsky from the afternoon well into the night. This is also the home of Soviet rock. The Leningrad Rock Club opened in 1981; Viktor Tsoi of Kino and Boris Grebenshchikov of Aquarium both came out of this city, and Tsoi worked as a stoker in a boiler room called Kamchatka, writing songs between shovelling coal. Young people here still love underground music, independent bookshops, little bars in old buildings and rooftops more than anywhere else.

[图]

[图]

Summer Petersburg is another world. From late May to mid-July are the white nights. At their brightest, in late June, the sun sets after ten in the evening and rises again after three in the morning, and in between it never really gets dark, the sky just turns a pale blue. The whole city seems to have collective insomnia. At midnight the embankments are packed: people drinking, playing guitar, kissing, while tour boats pass under the bridges one after another. After one in the morning the bridges over the Neva rise one by one to let cargo ships through, the banks crowd with people waiting to watch, and when the spans lift there is applause and cheering. Miss the last bridge and you wait on the wrong side until morning. At the end of June there is also Scarlet Sails, when a ship with red sails glides down the Neva through fireworks to celebrate school graduates.

[图]

[图]

On the July trip I happened on the midnight White Nights marathon across Palace Bridge. Thousands of runners streamed past along the Neva and in front of the Winter Palace, under lit street lamps in a sky that refused to get dark, with people cheering at the roadside and runners waving at the camera and throwing their arms wide, like a festival. I barely slept those few days. It was light all the time, and sleep felt like a waste.

[图]

[图]

By day, the Gulf of Finland on the west side of the city has a different kind of quiet. People wade barefoot into the cool water, someone sits on the rocks for a whole evening, and the stones on the beach have been stacked into little towers. The Baltic is a grey-blue, not especially pretty, but very calm.

[图]

Winter is the exact opposite. At the shortest days in December there is less than six hours of daylight: it gets light at ten and dark at four, and most days the sky is one flat grey. My January trip fell on Orthodox Christmas. It snowed for days and the Gulf of Finland froze into an endless white plain. Some people set up little stools and fished through holes in the ice; someone just walked off alone towards the middle of all that white. Children rolled in the snow with big dogs going wild beside them, and the churches were full of people at Christmas services, a sea of candles. Winter Petersburg is quiet and inward-looking, and it is the most Petersburg it ever gets.

[图]

[图]

[图]

Petersburg is often called the most European city in Russia, and that is true. The scale of the streets, the canals, the cafés, the well-dressed young people, the respect for art and personal space can make you think for a moment you are in Amsterdam or Paris. But stay longer and you realise it is not Western Europe after all. The sky here is too low, the winter too long, the history too heavy. Pushkin wrote about a little clerk who loses everything in a flood and goes mad; Gogol wrote about a little man who loses his overcoat and dies of grief; Dostoevsky has his hero lie in fever in a garret near Haymarket Square, and calls this the most abstract and premeditated city on earth. There is a faint sadness in Petersburgers: a little sobriety even in the middle of the fun, an awareness, even while celebrating, that the celebration will end. Maybe the white nights are so wild precisely because everyone remembers that winter will soon be back.

[图]

The poet Joseph Brodsky was expelled from the Soviet Union and never came back, not even at the end, yet as a young man he wrote that he would choose neither country nor graveyard, but would come to Vasilyevsky Island to die. That is probably how many Petersburgers feel about their city: they complain about its weather, its damp, its disappointments, but it is the only one.

[图]

IV. A city written in stone

Petersburg is a planned city. It has none of Moscow's ring-within-ring, layer-upon-layer chaos: the streets are straight, the squares are wide, and the buildings line up neatly along the water. Peter brought in architects from Italy, France and Germany, and over the next two centuries Trezzini, Rastrelli, Quarenghi, Rossi, Montferrand and others took the Baroque, Neoclassicism and the Empire style about as far as they could go. The street Rossi designed is 22 metres wide, its buildings are 22 metres high, and it is 220 metres long, the proportions locked together exactly. Even more important, from 1844 the city strictly enforced a rule that no civilian building could be taller than the Winter Palace. So the skyline is almost flat, broken only by church domes and the gold spires of the Admiralty and the Peter and Paul Cathedral. From up high it looks like a quiet sea of stone.

[图]

St Isaac's Cathedral is the biggest rock in that sea. The French architect Montferrand spent forty years on it, from 1818 to 1858. More than a hundred monolithic granite columns were shipped from quarries across the Gulf of Finland, and the gilded dome is said to have taken over a hundred kilograms of gold. In Soviet times it was a Museum of Atheism, with a Foucault pendulum hanging under the dome. Climb up to the colonnade and the whole centre lies at your feet: the Admiralty spire, the Winter Palace, the Peter and Paul Fortress, and far away by the sea, the Lakhta Center.

[图]

The one building that refuses to blend in with all this European architecture is the Church of the Savior on Spilled Blood. In 1881 Alexander II was mortally wounded by a bomb thrown by revolutionaries beside the Griboyedov Canal and died the same day. His son built this church on the spot where he was attacked, with Moscow-style onion domes and coloured brick. Almost every inch inside is mosaic, more than seven thousand square metres of it. On a winter evening, once the lights come on, it looks like a fairy tale in the snow.

[图]

Nevsky Prospekt is the city's spine, with the Admiralty at one end and the Alexander Nevsky Monastery at the other. Kazan Cathedral copied the curved colonnade of St Peter's in Rome, and Kutuzov, the commander who beat Napoleon, is buried inside. Across the street, the Singer Building carries a glass globe on its roof; it was built for the American Singer sewing machine company and is now the city's best-known bookshop, Dom Knigi. Around New Year the whole avenue is strung with lights, and from above it is a glowing river.

[图]

[图]

Go further in and there is the Trinity Cathedral of the Izmailovsky Regiment with its blue domes scattered with gold stars, Rastrelli's blue-and-white Smolny Cathedral, and bridge after little bridge over the canals; "Venice of the North" is not an empty nickname. The Griboyedov Canal winds down to Haymarket Square, which is Crime and Punishment territory: from his garret to the old moneylender's flat, Raskolnikov walks, the book says, exactly seven hundred and thirty steps.

[图]

Art here is not decoration, it is the air. The Hermitage holds three million objects (I wrote a separate story about it), the Russian Museum hangs Repin and Aivazovsky, and the Mariinsky premiered The Sleeping Beauty and The Nutcracker. Pushkin, Gogol, Dostoevsky, Akhmatova, Nabokov, Brodsky; Tchaikovsky, Rimsky-Korsakov, Shostakovich: nearly half the names in Russian cultural history are bound up with this city.

[图]

On the July trip I went to the Alexander Nevsky Monastery at the end of Nevsky. A walk round its cemeteries is a who's who: Dostoevsky, Tchaikovsky and Mussorgsky are all buried here. I stopped at a granite tomb whose sign read "Л. ЭЙЛЕР 1707–1783": the mathematician Leonhard Euler, who worked at the Petersburg Academy of Sciences for more than thirty years in total and died here. Not far away is a gravestone carved with Chinese characters, belonging to Nikita Bichurin, Father Iakinf, the founder of Russian sinology, who lived in Beijing for over a decade and was the first to translate many Chinese classics into Russian. Reading eight Chinese characters praising a lifetime of tireless work, in a Russian cemetery, was a strange and lovely feeling.

[图]

The only thing that breaks the skyline is the Lakhta Center, finished in 2019: 462 metres, the tallest building in Europe. It was originally meant to go up across the river from the centre, but residents and UNESCO fought it all the way because it would ruin the historic skyline, and in the end it was moved out to the seashore in the north-west. I rather like that ending: the city is willing to take in new things, as long as they leave its old rules alone.

[图]

In the end, Saint Petersburg is a city that should never have existed: built on a swamp, with long dark winters, besieged almost to death, and yet still standing, beautiful with all its might. It has a European skeleton, a Russian soul, and a sorrowful pride that belongs to it alone. Every time I leave, I feel sure I will be back.

[图]

stories.title: 北极圈之内，太阳不升起的城市
stories.titleEn: Murmansk, where the sun never rises
stories.text:
摩尔曼斯克是北极圈里最大的城市，也是一座港口城市。北纬69度，墨西哥湾暖流一路北上，让这里的港口冬天也不封冻。我们去的时候是1月初，正好赶上极夜的尾巴。

[图]

去之前我对极夜的想象，是一天24小时都黑漆漆的。真到了才知道，极夜原来并不是一直天黑，而是太阳不会升起。中午前后有几个小时，天会亮起来，太阳就藏在地平线下面，整片天空被染成一种很深、很透的蓝，地平线那一圈泛着橙色和粉色，像日出，又像日落。就这样持续一两个小时，再慢慢暗回去，一整天都像是在黄昏里。

说实话，出发前我对零下二十度没有任何概念，穿了三件就去了。买的红眼航班，天还没亮就落地，走出机场的那一瞬间，脸像被人扇了一巴掌，鼻子里的水汽瞬间结冰扎得人生疼，我就知道事情不对劲了。

[图]

更要命的是，到了市区，我们找不到民宿在哪。对着导航转了一圈又一圈，楼都长得差不多，门全锁着，天是黑的，街上一个人也没有。没有地方可去，只能在大街上到处走，越走越冷，手指和脚趾慢慢没了知觉。那一刻我是真的以为自己要冻死在北极了。

最后救了我们的是一位天没亮就起来遛狗的居民。零下二十度，凌晨，遛狗，离谱。等那人牵着狗回来开楼门的时候，我们厚着脸皮跟了进去。上锁的居民楼过道里虽然也没有暖气，但我们在楼道里一直待到天亮，好歹保住了小命。

后来几天在街上观察，发现这里的居民仿佛都对寒冷免疫了。我裹得像个球，帽子、围巾、口罩一样不少，还是冻得直哆嗦；他们穿着单薄的外套，有的连帽子都不戴，慢悠悠地走在雪里，有说有笑。难道真的变异了吗……

[图]

城市边的山丘上，站着阿廖沙。

它的正式名字叫「苏联北极地区保卫者纪念碑」，1974年落成：一个披着军大衣、肩上挎着枪的士兵，雕像本身35米多，连底座有40多米高，落成时是全苏联第二高的雕塑。二战时德军从挪威打过来，前线就停在离摩尔曼斯克不远的地方，一僵持就是三年多。城里大部分房子都被炸毁了，这座城市却始终没有陷落。阿廖沙面朝西边，望着当年战线所在的方向。脚下有一团长明火，雪下了一层又一层，它却一直烧着。

[图]

我们去的那天雾很大，树上挂满了霜，站在山顶往下看，城市和海湾都淡在一片白里。

[图]

另一个有意思的故事是谢苗。

谢苗是一只猫，1987年，一户摩尔曼斯克人家开车经过莫斯科回家，带着家里的暹罗猫谢苗。谢苗在莫斯科跑丢了，怎么找都找不到。六年半以后的某一天，一只瘦得不成样子的猫出现在他们家门口，是谢苗。从莫斯科到摩尔曼斯克，将近两千公里，没人知道它是怎么走回来的。

2013年，城里给它立了一座铜像：一只小猫，扛着一根挑着小包袱的棍子，像刚刚走完那段漫长的路。我们是晚上去的，它身上落满了雪，每个来参观的人都在它头上浇水，结了一层厚厚的冰。

[图]

说回我们的民宿。那是一间温馨的小屋，经历过第一天早上的那场「生死劫」，它给了我满满的安全感。每天早晨醒来，窗外是一片蓝，楼顶、树枝、街道全都银装素裹，安安静静的。我站在窗边发呆，如果能一直在这里待下去就好了。

[图]

到了中午前后，天边会变成橙色和粉色。整个世界都是干净的：空气是干净的，雪是干净的，连路也是干净的。在外面走一整天回来，鞋子比我自己洗过还干净。

[图]

我们去的时候刚好是新年期间。在俄罗斯，新年比圣诞节隆重得多，假期从元旦一直放到1月上旬。市中心的广场上搭起了冰屋和巨大的灯饰，灯一亮，金色和蓝色铺满了整条街。穿着雪姑娘衣服的姑娘站在雪里和人合影，小孩在灯下的雪地里跑来跑去。北极的大都市过起年来，一点也不冷清。

[图]

[图]

吃的必须说说帝王蟹，真的好吃，是我吃过第二好吃的海鲜。第一名是在神户吃到的天妇罗。话说，天妇罗算海鲜吗？

[图]

港口边停着列宁号，世界上第一艘核动力破冰船，1959年开始服役，在北冰洋上破了三十年的冰，退役以后就停在这里，成了博物馆。

[图]

列宁号附近，立着一块写着这座城市经纬坐标的牌子。我们路过的时候，正好有人在那里求婚，单膝跪在雪地里，周围的人都停下来看。北极圈里，零下二十度，很浪漫。

[图]

旁边的栏杆上挂着一排爱情锁，每一把都裹着厚厚的冰渣。情侣们靠在栏杆边依偎、接吻，呼出来的气一下就变成了白雾。

[图]

当然，来摩尔曼斯克绕不开的还有追极光，和去巴伦支海边的捷里别尔卡，这又是和城市生活完全不同的另一段故事了。

[图]

太阳不升起的天空，冻到怀疑人生的清晨，楼道里的那几个小时，走了两千公里回家的猫，窗外的蓝，冰渣下的锁。这座城市给我的这些独特体验，真的很难忘。

[图]
stories.textEn:
Murmansk is the largest city inside the Arctic Circle, and a port city. It sits at 69 degrees north, yet the last of the Gulf Stream reaches this far and keeps the harbour from freezing even in winter. We went in early January, just catching the tail end of the polar night.

[图]

Before the trip, I imagined the polar night as twenty-four hours of darkness. It turns out the polar night is not endless dark; it is simply that the sun never rises. For a few hours around noon the sky does get light. The sun stays hidden below the horizon, the whole sky turns a deep, clear blue, and the horizon glows orange and pink, like sunrise, or sunset. It lasts an hour or two, then slowly fades back. The whole day feels like dusk.

Then there is the cold. Honestly, before I left I had no idea what minus twenty actually meant, and I went in three layers. We took a red-eye, landed before dawn, and the moment I stepped out of the airport it felt like a slap across the face. I knew something had gone wrong.

[图]

Worse, once we got into the city we couldn't find our apartment. We circled again and again with the map, every building looked the same, every door was locked, it was dark, and there was no one on the street. With nowhere to go we just kept walking, colder and colder, until I could no longer feel my fingers or toes. At that point I genuinely thought I was going to freeze to death in the Arctic.

In the end we were saved by a dog. More precisely, by a local who had got up before dawn to walk it. Minus twenty, the middle of the night, walking the dog. Absurd. When they came back and unlocked the building door, we shamelessly followed them in. The locked building had heating, and we stayed in the stairwell until it got light. At least we survived.

Over the next few days I watched people on the street, and the locals seemed completely immune to the cold. I was wrapped up like a ball, hat, scarf and mask, and still shivering; they strolled through the snow in thin jackets, some without even a hat, chatting and laughing. Have they actually mutated?

[图]

On a hill at the edge of the city stands Alyosha.

Its official name is the Monument to the Defenders of the Soviet Arctic, unveiled in 1974: a soldier in a greatcoat with a rifle over his shoulder. The figure alone is over 35 metres tall, more than 40 with the pedestal, and when it opened it was the second-tallest statue in the Soviet Union. In the Second World War the German army came in from Norway, and the front stopped not far from Murmansk and stayed there for more than three years. Most of the city's houses were bombed out, yet the city never fell. Alyosha faces west, towards where the front line used to be. At his feet burns an eternal flame; snow falls layer after layer, and it keeps burning.

[图]

The day we went it was very foggy, the trees were covered in frost, and from the top of the hill the city and the bay faded into white.

[图]

The other thing I remember is Semyon.

Semyon is a cat. In 1987 a family from Murmansk was driving home through Moscow with their Siamese cat, Semyon. He ran off in Moscow and they never found him. Six and a half years later, a cat so thin he was barely recognisable turned up at their door. It was Semyon. Moscow to Murmansk is nearly two thousand kilometres, and nobody knows how he walked home.

In 2013 the city gave him a bronze statue: a little cat carrying a stick with a bundle tied to the end, as if he had just finished that long road. We went at night, and he was covered in snow.

[图]

Back to our apartment. It was a cosy little place, and after that first morning's brush with death it made me feel completely safe. Every morning I woke up to blue outside the window, the rooftops, branches and streets all dressed in white and perfectly quiet. I would often just stand at the window, thinking how nice it would be to stay here forever.

[图]

Around noon the horizon turns orange and pink. The whole world is clean: the air is clean, the snow is clean, even the roads are clean. After a whole day of walking outside, my shoes were cleaner than if I had washed them myself.

[图]

We happened to be there over New Year. In Russia, New Year is a much bigger deal than Christmas, and the holiday runs from the first of January well into the second week. The central square was filled with ice houses and huge light displays; when the lights came on, gold and blue covered the whole street. A girl dressed as the Snow Maiden stood in the snow taking photos with people, and kids ran around in the snow under the lights. An Arctic city celebrating New Year is anything but quiet.

[图]

[图]

As for food, I have to mention the king crab. It was genuinely delicious, the second-best seafood I have ever had. First place goes to the tempura I had in Kobe. Then again, does tempura even count as seafood?

[图]

At the harbour lies the Lenin, the world's first nuclear-powered surface ship. It went into service in 1959, broke ice in the Arctic Ocean for thirty years, and since retiring has been moored here as a museum.

[图]

Near the Lenin stands a sign with the city's coordinates. As we walked past, someone was proposing right there, down on one knee in the snow, with people stopping to watch. Inside the Arctic Circle, at minus twenty. Very romantic.

[图]

On the railing nearby hangs a row of love locks, each one coated in a thick crust of ice. Couples leaned against the railing, holding each other and kissing, their breath turning instantly to white mist. It had a real feeling to it.

[图]

Of course, no trip to Murmansk is complete without chasing the northern lights, or going out to Teriberka on the Barents Sea. Both deserve a story of their own, so I'll leave them for later.

[图]

A sky where the sun never rises, a morning so cold it made me question my life choices, a few hours in a stairwell, a cat who walked two thousand kilometres home, the blue outside the window, the locks under the ice. The things this city gave me are hard to forget.

[图]
